title: 天順四年會試錄
text:
會試錄序
天順四年春二月當禮部會
試天下貢士之期知貢舉左
侍郎臣榦等前期以考試官
請
上以命臣原臣潛而為同考者臣
鑑臣宣臣璵臣本臣濬臣直
===
臣讓臣鉉臣宜臣宗臣俊臣
禹錫監試者臣越臣琛以是月
七日偕諸執事入院內外一
心防範加密至期命題初場
試義次場試論詔誥表判終
場試策糊名易書一遵故事
臣等悉心校閱夜以繼旦如

punctuated:
會試錄序

天順四年春二月，當禮部會試天下貢士之期。知貢舉左侍郎臣榦等，前期以考試官請，上以命臣原、臣潛；而為同考者：臣鑑、臣宣、臣璵、臣本、臣濬、臣直、臣讓、臣鉉、臣宜、臣宗、臣俊、臣禹錫；監試者：臣越、臣琛。以是月七日，偕諸執事入院，內外一心，防範加密。至期命題：初場試義，次場試論、詔、誥、表、判，終場試策。糊名易書，一遵故事。臣等悉心校閱，夜以繼旦，如
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

In the second month of spring in the fourth year of the Tianshun reign [1460], the time arrived for the Ministry of Rites to conduct the Metropolitan Examination of tribute scholars from across the realm. Prior to the date, Administrator of the Tribute Examination and Left Vice Minister Your Servant Gan and others memorialized to request the appointment of Examiners. His Majesty commanded Your Servant Yuan and Your Servant Qian to serve as Examiners; while those serving as Associate Examiners were Your Servant Jian, Your Servant Xuan, Your Servant Yu, Your Servant Ben, Your Servant Jun, Your Servant Zhi, Your Servant Rang, Your Servant Xuan, Your Servant Yi, Your Servant Zong, Your Servant Jun, and Your Servant Yuxi; and the Surveillance Commissioners for the Examination were Your Servant Yue and Your Servant Chen. On the seventh day of this month, together with the various functionaries, we entered the examination compound; those inside and outside were of one mind, and security precautions were made still tighter. When the scheduled days arrived, the questions were set: the first session tested expositions of the Classics and Four Books; the second session tested discourses, imperial edicts, imperial mandates, memorials, and legal judgments; and the final session tested policy essays. The sealing of candidates' names and the recopying of papers complied entirely with established precedent. Your Servants devoted our whole minds to reading and grading the papers, working through the night into the dawn, like…

title: 天順四年會試錄
text:
揀金於砂求玉於璞非精粹
者弗取乃於三千餘卷得中
式者凡百五十爰列其名氏
及表其文理尤純者為會試
錄錄成僉謂宜有序而以屬
原切惟建學養士唐虞三代
已然雖當時科目未設而四
===
門之闢三載之大比莫非進
賢之路厥後若漢唐宋亦皆
有學而取士類非一科我
朝學校徧於天下設科取士必
試以義論詔誥表判策者盖
因歷代明經射策博學宏詞
明法諸科之制合而為一宜

有學而取士類非一科我
朝學校徧於天下設科取士必

因歷代明經射策博學宏詞
明法諸科之制合而爲一宜
punctuated:
揀金於砂，求玉於璞，非精粹者弗取。乃於三千餘卷得中式者凡百五十。爰列其名氏，及表其文理尤純者為《會試錄》。錄成，僉謂宜有序，而以屬原。
切惟建學養士，唐、虞、三代已然。雖當時科目未設，而四門之闢、三載之大比，莫非進賢之路。厥後若漢、唐、宋，亦皆有學，而取士類非一科。我朝學校徧於天下，設科取士，必試以義、論、詔、誥、表、判、策者，盖因歷代明經、射策、博學宏詞、明法諸科之制，合而為一，宜
translation_en:
… panning gold from sand or seeking jade within unworked stone, selecting nothing that was not pure and refined. Thus, out of more than three thousand examination papers, we obtained a total of one hundred and fifty candidates who met the standard. We then listed their names and surnames, and highlighted the essays whose style and reasoning were especially pure, to compile the Record of the Metropolitan Examination (Huishi lu). When the record was completed, everyone said that there ought to be a preface and entrusted the task to me, [Lü] Yuan.
I humbly reflect that establishing schools to nurture scholars was already practiced in the eras of Tang [Yao], Yu [Shun], and the Three Dynasties. Although formal examination categories had not yet been instituted at that time, the opening of the gates of the four quarters and the great triennial comparison of talent were nonetheless avenues for advancing the worthy. Thereafter, dynasties such as the Han, Tang, and Song also all maintained schools, yet they generally selected scholars through more than a single examination category. In our dynasty, schools are spread throughout the realm, and in establishing the examinations to select scholars, candidates are invariably tested in expositions of the classics, discourses, imperial edicts, imperial mandates, memorials, legal judgments, and policy essays. This is because the system draws upon the various examination categories of successive dynasties—such as Classicists (mingjing), Conjecturing Policies (shece), Erudite Literatus (boxue hongci), and Legalists (mingfa)—and combines them into one. It is fitting…

title: 天順四年會試錄
text:
乎得賢之盛非漢唐宋之可
及也夫治天下以賢為本得
賢雖係於教養選舉而尤本
於上之人躬行之實故光天
之下則黎獻共臣丕釐耿命
則宅俊克即徵諸古可見已
仰惟我
===
朝
列聖相承德隆化洽俊乂登庸後
先相望今
皇上重膺
佑命躬行
天德仁以覆九區義以正百辟
由是聲教四訖猶日月照臨
alt_text:
乎得賢之盛非漢唐宋之可
及也夫治天下以賢爲本得
賢雖係於敎養選擧而尤本
於上之人躬行之實故光天
之下則黎獻共臣丕釐耿命
則宅俊克卽徵諸古可見已
仰惟我
===
朝
列聖相承德隆化洽俊乂登庸後
先相望今
皇上重膺
佑命躬行
天德仁以覆九區義以正百辟
由是聲教四訖猶日月照臨
punctuated: 乎得賢之盛，非漢、唐、宋之可及也。夫治天下以賢為本，得賢雖係於教養選舉，而尤本於上之人躬行之實。故光天之下，則黎獻共臣；丕釐耿命，則宅俊克即，徵諸古可見已。仰惟我朝列聖相承，德隆化洽，俊乂登庸，後先相望。今皇上重膺佑命，躬行天德，仁以覆九區，義以正百辟。由是聲教四訖，猶日月照臨，
translation_en: … that the abundance of worthy talent obtained cannot be matched by the Han, Tang, or Song dynasties. Now, governing the realm takes worthy talent as its foundation; although obtaining worthy men depends upon nurturing through education and selection through examinations, it is rooted even more deeply in the reality of personal practice by the ruler above. Thus, "under the bright sky," "the wise among the multitude together become subjects"; and when "grandly administering the glorious mandate," "those settled in offices of eminence are able to take up their posts"—verifying this against antiquity, it can clearly be seen. Looking up in reverence, we reflect that in our dynasty, successive sage emperors have inherited the throne one after another; their virtue has been lofty and their transforming influence all-pervasive, so that men of outstanding talent have been elevated and employed, following closely upon one another in an unbroken line. Now His Majesty the Emperor has once again received the Mandate assisted by Heaven and personally practices heavenly virtue, using benevolence to shelter the nine regions and righteousness to rectify the hundred officials. Consequently, his prestigious instruction reaches to the four quarters, just like the sun and moon shining down from above, …

title: 天順四年會試錄
text:
雷風鼓舞普天率土莫不尊
親則夫士承教養而應選舉
欲以行其志達其道者固宜
若是之多也且臣等取士惟
擇其文理之純者盖以文即
其言而言乃心之聲行之表
言純乎理則其用心於內有
===
志於行槩可驗矣然古聖賢
之訓以博學審問慎思明辨
篤行為當務諸士子純理之
文要皆學問思辨之所能而
篤行之功可不益加勉乎苟
能勉勉弗忘將見存心制行
悉顧其言而立

志於行槩可驗矣然古聖賢
之訓以博學審問慎思明辨
篤行爲當務諸士子純理之
文要皆學問思辨之所能而
篤行之功可不益加勉乎茍
能勉勉弗忘將見存心制行
悉顧其言而立
punctuated: 雷風鼓舞，普天率土莫不尊親。則夫士承教養而應選舉，欲以行其志、達其道者，固宜若是之多也。且臣等取士，惟擇其文理之純者，盖以文即其言，而言乃心之聲、行之表；言純乎理，則其用心於內、有志於行，槩可驗矣。然古聖賢之訓，以博學、審問、慎思、明辨、篤行為當務。諸士子純理之文，要皆學、問、思、辨之所能，而篤行之功，可不益加勉乎？苟能勉勉弗忘，將見存心制行悉顧其言，而立
translation_en: …and as thunder and wind rouse all things, so that throughout the whole world and to the utmost bounds of the land there is none who does not revere and love Him. Thus it is only fitting that there should be so many scholars who, having received instruction and nourishment, respond to the selection for office, desiring to carry out their aspirations and put their Way into practice. Furthermore, in selecting candidates, Your servants have chosen only those whose literary expression and moral principle are pure. This is because literary composition is simply one's words, and words are the voice of the mind and the outward manifestation of conduct; when one's words are pure in principle, the devotion of one's mind within and one's aspiration toward right conduct can generally be verified thereby. Yet the teachings of the ancient sages and worthies hold that extensive study, accurate inquiry, careful reflection, clear discrimination, and earnest practice are the essential duties. The compositions of pure principle produced by the candidates are, in sum, what can be achieved through study, inquiry, reflection, and discrimination; how, then, could they not exert themselves even further in the effort of earnest practice? If they can strive tirelessly without forgetting, we shall see them preserve their minds and regulate their conduct in complete accordance with their words, and when they take their stand…

title: 天順四年會試錄
text:
朝涖官允為名臣若然則豈特
無負
國家教養選舉之意而今日預
考校者亦有榮也否則取譏
於世謂科目不足以得人其
為名教玷也大矣諸士子尚
其勗哉
===
翰林院學士奉議大夫吕原
謹序
alt_text:
朝廷官允爲名臣若然則豈特
無負
國家教養選舉之意而今日預
考校者亦有榮也否則取譏
於世謂科目不足以得人其
爲名教玷也大矣諸士子尚
其勖哉
翰林院學士奉議大夫呂原
謹序
punctuated:
朝涖官，允為名臣。若然，則豈特無負國家教養選舉之意，而今日預考校者亦有榮也。否則，取譏於世，謂科目不足以得人，其為名教玷也大矣。諸士子尚其勗哉！
翰林院學士、奉議大夫吕原謹序。
translation_en:
…at court and assuming official posts, they will truly become renowned ministers. If this is so, then not only will they not fail the state's intention in nurturing, educating, and selecting them, but those of us participating in the examination and evaluation today will also share in the honor. Otherwise, they will incur the ridicule of the world, which will say that the examination system is insufficient for obtaining capable men, and the blemish upon Confucian teachings will be great indeed. May all you scholars strive your utmost!

Respectfully prefaced by Lü Yuan 吕原, Hanlin Academician and Grand Master for Proper Consultation.

translation_en:
Metropolitan Examination of the Fourth Year of the Tianshun Era (1460)

Administrator of the Memorialized Examinations (知貢舉官):
Zou Gan 鄒幹, Grand Master for Proper Consultation (正議大夫), Aide to Governance (資治尹), and Left Vice Minister of Rites (禮部左侍郎) [courtesy name Zongsheng 宗盛, a native of Yuhang County, Zhejiang, and a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the jiwei year (1439)].

Examiners (考試官):
Lü Yuan 呂原, Chancellor of the Hanlin Academy (翰林院學士) and Grand Master forRendered Service (奉議大夫) [courtesy name Fengyuan 逢原, a native of Xiushui County, Zhejiang, and a metropolitan graduate of the renxu year (1442)].
Ke Qian 柯潛, Grand Master for Admonishment (奉訓大夫), Vice Director of the Seals Office (尚寶司少卿), and concurrently Senior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy (翰林院修撰) [courtesy name Mengshi 孟時, a native of Putian County, Fujian, and a metropolitan graduate of the xinwei year (1451)].

Associate Examiners (同考試官):
Chen Jian 陳鑑, Senior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy (翰林院修撰) and Gentleman for Fostering Service (承務郎) [courtesy name Jixi 緝熙, a native of Changzhou County, Southern Metropolitan Area (Zhili), and a metropolitan graduate of the wuchen year (1448)].

title: 天順四年會試錄
text:
第壹塲
四書
君子之於天下也無適也無莫也義之與
比
知遠之近知風之自知微之顯
或勞心或勞力勞心者治人勞力者治於
人治於人者食人治人者食於人
易
貞固足以幹事
===
或益之十朋之龜弗克違永貞吉
繼之者善也成之者性也仁者見之謂之
仁知者見之謂之知
是以立天之道曰陰與陽立地之道曰柔
與剛立人之道曰仁與義兼三才而
兩之故易六畫而成卦
書
臣哉鄰哉鄰哉臣哉
官不及私昵惟其能爵罔及惡德惟其賢

四書
君子之於天下也，無適也，無莫也，義之與比。
知遠之近，知風之自，知微之顯。
或勞心，或勞力；勞心者治人，勞力者治於人；治於人者食人，治人者食於人。

貞固足以幹事。

是以立天之道，曰陰與陽；立地之道，曰柔與剛；立人之道，曰仁與義。兼三才而兩之，故易六畫而成卦。

First Session

Four Books
"The superior man, in his dealings with the world, does not set his mind either for anything or against anything; what is right he will follow." (Analects 4.10)
"He knows how what is distant lies in what is near, knows where the wind comes from, and knows how what is minute becomes manifest." (Doctrine of the Mean 33)
"Some labor with their minds, and some labor with their strength. Those who labor with their minds govern others; those who labor with their strength are governed by others. Those who are governed by others support them; those who govern others are supported by them." (Mencius 3A.4)

Book of Changes (Yi)
"Firmness and correctness are sufficient to manage affairs." (Qian, Wenyan)
"Someone increases him; ten pairs of tortoises cannot oppose it. Constant perseverance brings good fortune." (Hexagram 42, Yi, Second Yin; or Hexagram 41, Sun, Fifth Yin)
"That which continues it is good; that which completes it is the nature. The benevolent see it and call it benevolence; the wise see it and call it wisdom." (Xici I.5)
"Therefore they established the Way of Heaven, calling it the dark (yin) and the light (yang); they established the Way of Earth, calling it the yielding and the firm; they established the Way of Man, calling it benevolence and righteousness. They combined these three powers and doubled them; therefore in the Changes six lines complete a hexagram." (Shuogua 2)

Book of Documents (Shu)
"My ministers! My associates! My associates! My ministers!" (Yi and Ji)
"Offices are not given to personal favorites, but only to the able; dignities are not conferred on men of evil virtue, but only on the worthy." (Charge to Yue II)

"Take thought for what is good before acting, and act only at the proper time."
"The King was in the new city. He performed the winter sacrifice for the new year, offering one red bull to King Wen and one red bull to King Wu. The King commanded that a brevet be prepared, and Yi recited the prayer on the brevet, announcing only that the Duke of Zhou would have a successor."
"The Mandate we have received is boundlessly auspicious, yet also great in its difficulties."

Classic of Poetry (Shi)
"My horses are colts, the six reins look as if moistened; I gallop and drive them, everywhere inquiring and taking counsel. My horses are dappled grays, the six reins are like silk; I gallop and drive them, everywhere inquiring and planning. My horses are white with black manes, the six reins are glossy; I gallop and drive them, everywhere inquiring and deliberating. My horses are grays with white-speckled legs, the six reins are well-balanced; I gallop and drive them, everywhere inquiring and consulting."
"By the Feng River grows the white millet; how could King Wu not take up the work? He bequeathed his plans to his grandsons, to give peace and support to his sons. Truly a sovereign was King Wu!"
"Only Zhong Shanfu neither devours the soft nor spits out the hard."
"Neithererring in reward nor excessive in punishment, they dared not be indolent or take leisure."

"Kindness in the father, filial piety in the son, gentleness in the elder brother, fraternal respect in the younger brother, righteousness in the husband, obedience in the wife, benevolence in elders, compliance in the young, humaneness in the ruler, and loyalty in the minister: these ten are called the principles of human righteousness."

隱瞞入官家産。

第參塲
策五道

問：人稟五行之秀以生，而其所以為人之道，五常而已。是道也，自脩身以至於為天下，不可一日而無。故任世道之責者，咸首務焉。洪惟我太祖高皇帝有申明五常之誥，宣宗章皇帝有纂輯《五倫》之書，其為世道計也至矣。稽之往古，在唐虞時，或「慎徽五典」，或「敬敷五教」，而又有「五品不遜」之言；在商周時，或「肇脩人紀」，或「重民五教」，而又有「彝倫攸叙」之說。乃若孔孟立言，亦有所謂…
translation_en:
Legal judgments (判語) [five items]:
1. Colluding with officials in close attendance at court (交結近侍官員).
2. Concealing family property subject to confiscation by the state (隱瞞入官家産).
3.Improperly releasing soldiers from active duty to rest (縱放軍人歇役).
4. Fraudulently instructing or inducing others to violate the law (詐教誘人犯法).
5. Weaving prohibited satin and silk fabrics (織造違禁段匹).

Third Session
Five Policy Questions (策)

Question: Human beings are born endowed with the finest essence of the Five Phases (五行), and the Way by which they are human consists simply in the Five Constant Virtues (五常). From cultivating the self all the way to governing the world, this Way cannot be dispensed with for a single day. Therefore, those who bear responsibility for the moral order of the world all make it their foremost task. We reflect with awe upon how Our Grand Progenitor, Emperor Gao (太祖高皇帝, the Hongwu Emperor), issued the Imperial Injunction Reiterating the Five Constant Virtues (申明五常之誥), and how Ancestor Xuanzong, Emperor Zhang (宣宗章皇帝, the Xuande Emperor), compiled the Book of the Five Human Relationships (五倫書); their concern for the moral order of the world was comprehensive indeed. Examining remote antiquity, in the times of Tang [Yao] and Yu [Shun], there was "carefully exemplifying the Five Canons" (慎徽五典) or "reverently spreading the Five Teachings" (敬敷五教), and there were also the words that "the five classes of relationships are not harmonious" (五品不遜); in the times of the Shang and Zhou dynasties, there was "initiating the cultivation of human moral standards" (肇脩人紀) or "attaching great importance to the people's Five Teachings" (重民五教), and there was also the doctrine of "the invariable human relationships being set in order" (彝倫攸叙). …what are called "the five universal ways of the world" and "the sage is the culmination of human relationships." Even so, is what is said in the imperial compilations of Our Dynasty the same as or different from what is said in the ancient Classics and commentaries? Now, how is it that the Five Constant Virtues, the Five Human Relationships, the Five Teachings, the Human Bonds, the Invariant Relationships, and the Universal Ways have different names? And how is it that "reiterating and clarifying," "carefully displaying," "reverently propagating," "initiating and cultivating," "attaching great weight to the people's [Five Teachings]," and "whereby they are brought into order" have different meanings? Can you enumerate them one by one and explain them in detail? You gentlemen have immersed your minds in the study of Principle for years and must be able to elucidate their purport; I hope you will set it forth in your essays.

Question: Knowing men is assuredly difficult, and employing men is also not easy; it has been so since antiquity. Thus, even with the wisdom of Yao, Gonggong and Gun were at court; even with the worthiness of Zhongkang, the Xi and He brothers neglected their duties—how much more so in later ages! From that time onward, there was one who knew a man would surely be able to secure the Liu clan, and one who knew a man could be relied upon in emergencies; some knew that a man was being framed by wicked flatterers, and some knew that a man was not an evildoer; there was also one who, when a commoner presented policy advice, knew that he could serve as chief minister in the future, as well as one who knew from a man's attendance at a banquet that he could be entrusted with great responsibilities, and one who knew from a man's memorializing on affairs that he could bring about Great Peace. Knowing men like this was discerning indeed—yet were occasions when they were not discerning? Furthermore, there was one who employed three men to accomplish a great enterprise, and one who appointed a Chamberlain for Law Enforcement so as to bring about a reputation for fairness; some cast aside old grudges and placed a man as Policy Critic, and some refused to curry personal favor while promoting a man to Left Aide; there was also one who, keenly intent on Great Peace, demanded results from his chief ministers, as well as [those who said] "dreaming and divining…

問：廉介之節、恬退之風，二者皆為士所當先，而有國者所當尚也。古者千駟弗視，萬鍾何加，廉介之節高矣。而其後也，有不貪為寶、暮夜却金、愧市白集、不持一硯者，可以廉介許之否乎？卧帷不易、龜鶴自隨，與夫食惟脫粟者，果孰優乎？古者士讓為大夫，大夫讓為卿，恬退之風盛矣。而其後也，有辭相灌園、恥於呈身、

… cannot compare to human judgment, or who relied precisely on classical learning for exhortation and lecturing. Employing men like this was fitting indeed; yet were there also instances where it was not fitting? These are all deeds of the heroic and righteous rulers of the Han, Tang, and Song, clearly recorded in the historical compilations. Can you examine their facts and discuss them in detail? At present, the Sacred Son of Heaven seeks worthy men from before dawn until after dark with true knowledge and penetrating insight, so that in obtaining worthies he ought to rival the splendor of antiquity. Yet among the ranks of the Nine卿 [Chief Ministers] there are still many vacant posts, and the Commandery Governors and Magistrates are not all upright and良 [capable] officials. Is it really so difficult to know them and to employ them? Or is there some other reason? Now, if we wished to consult all the people of the state, I privately fear there would not be sufficient leisure; if we had each person recommend those whom he knows, there would be the worry of partiality. You students have studied antiquity in preparation for entering office and must hold thoroughly fitting views; set them forth without concealment.

Question: The integrity of incorruptible scrupulousness and the ethos of tranquil retirement—both of these are what scholars ought to put first, and what rulers of states ought to esteem. In antiquity, there were those who would not so much as look at a thousand teams of cuatro-horses, and who asked what ten thousand *zhong* of grain could add to them; the integrity of incorruptible scrupulousness was lofty indeed. In later times, there were those who regarded non-covetousness as their treasure, who refused gold in the dead of night, who were ashamed to buy the *Collected Works of Bai [Juyi]*, or who did not carry away a single inkstone—can these be granted recognition for incorruptible scrupulousness or not? Between one who did not replace his bed curtains, one who was accompanied only by a tortoise and a crane, and one who ate only unhulled grain, who was truly superior? In antiquity, servicemen yielded before becoming Grand Masters, and Grand Masters yielded before becoming Chief Ministers; the ethos of tranquil retirement flourished indeed. In later times, there were those who declined the post of Counsellor-in-Chief to water gardens, who were ashamed to present themselves in person, …

…bravely retreating from the rushing current, or hanging up one's official cap before growing old—can such men be praised for tranquil modesty? And between those who requested to return to Western Luo or refused to put themselves forward, and the one who retired in old age to Mount Zhong, who was truly the worthier? At present, there are statutes for honoring incorruptibility, yet the practice of cornering the market for profit still persists; there are laws for curbing private favoritism, yet the custom of bowing to the dust of the powerful has not ceased. If we definitely wish to transform greed and venality into incorruptible integrity, and change restless competition into tranquil modesty, how may this be achieved? Please pour forth what you hold in your hearts, and do not say, "In knowing the past and knowing the present, I am not as good as Gao Qi."

Question: To read all the books in the world and know all the affairs in the world—this is what is meant by an outstanding talent who understands the exigencies of the times. I venture to raise the most essential affairs and ask about them. Among our present concerns: the frontiers are not yet at peace, though we have generals for defense; criminal cases are not yet cleared, though there are imperial decrees for judicial review; widowers and widows are displaced, and we repeatedly relieve and succor them; bandits and thieves are not yet quelled, and we strictly prohibit and arrest them; and as for facilitating grain transport by water and relieving famine, there are regulations to adjust them as needed. Why is it that although these measures have been practiced for a long time, their results are not yet very evident? Yet these are merely the lesser matters; among affairs worth discussing, there are others even greater than these. Suppose we wish to completely reform frivolity and superficiality into honest simplicity, completely drive out heterodoxies so people return to ritual and righteousness, completely lead idle and lazy people to be diligent in agriculture and sericulture, and completely transform those who eat fine rice and wear brocade so that they revere filial piety and fraternal love—is there truly a way to do this, or not? Or will…

translation_en:
…consider that if even implementing the lesser measures has failed to take effect, there is no leisure yet to deliberate upon the greater ones? Or will one consider that there is indeed a way to handle the greater matters, so that the lesser ones are not worth worrying over? Or, because both bear upon governance and moral transformation, should one not choose between what is great and what is small, but rather undertake them together? Do not indulge in pedantic and impractical talk; I wish you to set forth what can actually be put into practice.

Question: Reverence (jing) is that whereby the learning of the sages completes both its beginning and its end, and its appearances in the Classics and commentaries are numerous. The Book of Documents (Shu) praises Yao as "reverently明 [bright/perspicacious] and sincerely courteous (qin ming yun gong)," yet praises Shun only as "mild and courteous (wen gong)." Could it be that Shun was incapable of such reverence (qin)? The Book of Odes (Shi) praises Tang, saying his "sagely reverence (jing) daily ascended," and praises King Wen, saying he was "continuously bright and reverent in his resting-places." Could it be that Tang and King Wen fell short of complete reverence (qin) and courtesy (gong)? The Book of Changes (Yi) says, "Reverence (jing) to straighten the internal; righteousness (yi) to square the external." Reverence and righteousness are both possessed within; why then divide them into internal and external? The Record of Rites (Li) says, "When the mind is grave (zhuang), the body is at ease; when the mind is solemn (su), the demeanor is reverent (jing)." Gravity and solemnity are manifested in one's demeanor; why then are they tied to the mind? The Zuo Commentary (Zhuan) says, "Reverence is the gathering together of virtue," and another commentary says, "Reverence consists in nourishing the spirit." How is it that reverence is able to gather virtue and nourish the spirit? When Confucius answered his disciples' questions about humaneness (ren), he constantly instructed them in terms of reverence; could it be that reverence is itself humaneness? When Zisi discussed how the Way cannot be departed from, he likewise followed it with reverence; could it be that reverence is itself the Way? Master Cheng said, "Concentrating on one thing is called reverence; going nowhere else is called being one." He also said, "When one is orderly, composed, stern, and solemn, the mind immediately becomes one." And he also said, "…

title: 天順四年會試錄
text:
涵養須用敬進學則在致知可究其旨
乎謝氏云敬是常惺惺法尹氏云敬者
其心收斂不容一物與程子之言有相
戾乎夫君子無所不用其敬學者於敬
誠所當務也其明言之以觀主敬之學

punctuated: 「涵養須用敬，進學則在致知。」可究其旨乎？謝氏云：「敬是常惺惺法。」尹氏云：「敬者，其心收斂不容一物。」與程子之言有相戾乎？夫君子無所不用其敬，學者於敬，誠所當務也。其明言之，以觀主敬之學。
translation_en: …“Nurturing the mind and nature requires using reverence; advancing in learning lies in extending knowledge.” Can you investigate the meaning of these sayings? Master Xie (Xie Liangzuo 謝良佐) says: “Reverence is the method of remaining constantly alert and awake.” Master Yin (Yin Tun 尹焞) says: “Reverence means the mind is gathered in and does not admit a single extraneous thing.” Are these in conflict with the words of Master Cheng? Now, the gentleman applies his reverence to everything, and for the scholar, reverence is truly what ought to be striven after. Explain this clearly, so that we may observe your learning in holding fast to reverence.

title: 天順四年會試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
君子之於天下也無適也無莫也義之與比
鄭紀
同考試官署員外郎陳批作者語多陳腐此篇
能化腐為新足見筆力高邁何忝
同考試官編修尹批作此題者多襲陳言令人厭
觀求其措詞簡古說理明白僅得此篇
同考試官編修李批題本平易作者於無適莫處
率用禁止意殊失本旨此篇理明詞暢足見講貫之學
考試官少卿柯批場屋中有此文足見所蘊
考試官學士呂批義得本旨而措辭簡當可取
君子之於世也不先事而有所倚惟隨事而制其宜
蓋事必有義也君子處天下之事惟義之是從初曷
嘗有所偏倚於其間哉今夫天下事無常形而理無
定在是以君子於日用常行之間應事接物之際固
未嘗先有專主之意而必於行亦未嘗先有不肯之
意而必於不行必於行則無一不可者固不可也必

In his dealings with the world, the superior man does not lean toward anything prior to the affair, but only determines what is appropriate in accordance with the affair itself. … on disapproval, so that nothing is permissible, is also wrong. That being so, does the mind of the noble man truly have nothing to govern it? One can only say that he follows righteousness alone. For righteousness is the regulation of the mind and the appropriateness of affairs. If an affair truly accords with righteousness, I will carry it out, paying no heed even if I might be suspected of following vulgar custom; if an affair is truly contrary to righteousness, I will not carry it out, feeling no concern even if I might be suspected of defying the multitude. Whether taking office or declining it, one looks solely to where righteousness lies, and extending this to all affairs in the world, there is none where it is not so. This is why the noble man is a noble man—how could ordinary people reach up to him! Yet if we discuss it further: the teachings of the Buddhists and Daoists hold that the mind should have nowhere to abide, which resembles having no predisposition for or against anything; yet they lack the Way to govern it, and ultimately degenerate into wild recklessness. Zimo's holding to the middle resembles righteousness; yet he is unable to observe principle in accordance with each affair, and ultimately ends in clinging to a single extreme. Both are harmful to our Way. Surely one must be without deliberate thought and without artificial action, wondrously grasping this principle in the mind, and be without predisposition for or against anything, practicing our righteousness in affairs—is this not the Way of the noble man, and the standard for scholars!

"Some labor with their minds, and some labor with their strength. Those who labor with their minds govern others; those who labor with their strength are governed by others. Those who are governed by others feed others; those who govern others are fed by others." [Mencius 3A.4]
Tong Sui 童璲

Social stations have the distinction of superior and inferior; human affairs have the principle of mutual dependence. Indeed, the gentleman labors with his mind and the lesser man labors with his strength; their stations inherently have the distinction of superior and inferior. Yet those below depend on those above to be governed, and those above depend on those below to be nourished—how then could the gentleman and the lesser man be of any detriment to one another? This is the meaning of the great worthy citing an ancient saying to refute a contemporary.

In the past, because Chen Xiang related the words of Xu Hang, Mencius had already debated them back and forth; and here he further cites an ancient saying to refute them, meaning to say: The world cannot be without gentlemen, and the business of the gentleman is to labor with his mind; the world cannot be without lesser men, and the business of the lesser man is to labor with his strength. Those who labor with their minds occupy positions above and oversee those below, cultivating their governance and clarifying their moral instruction, thereby governing others; those who labor with their strength occupy positions below and serve those above, heeding only the governance and following only the instruction, thereby being governed by others. Precisely because they are governed by others, they pay the taxes of the well-field lands and supply the needs of the public authorities—is this not feeding others? Precisely because they govern others, they have no leisure to plow alongside the people and yet enjoy their food, and do not busy themselves with cooking morning and evening meals and yet rely on their nourishment—is this not being fed by others?

Alas! When the gentleman labors with his mind, without the lesser man he has no means to be nourished; when the lesser man labors with his strength, without the gentleman he has no means to be governed. Exchanging these with one another is just like the farmer and the potter or smith exchanging grain for implements and vessels: it is whereby they mutually sustain one another, and not whereby they are a detriment to one another. 同考試官學正閻　批〔易卷五百有餘作此題者主見不一令人厭觀此作體認明而措詞健故表而出之〕
王璠
而成卦
是以立天之道曰陰與陽立地之道曰柔與剛
立人之道曰仁與義兼三才而兩之故易六畫
punctuated:
之靈，莫不有知，而天下之事，莫不有理。惟於理之正者，知之而不能守，故其於事亦無所依以立也。君子知其然，既有以知之，則必有以守之。如事親者其事，而仁則其正理也，君子真知乎此，而固守之不失，則事親之事依之而立矣；從兄者其事，而義則其正理也，君子灼見乎此，而堅持之不移，則從兄之事依之而立矣。推而至於天下之事，莫不皆然。孰謂事之所依以立者，有不在於貞固者乎？聖人推明人事之知，至此無餘蘊矣。或疑《文言》此節，曰「體仁」、「嘉會」、「利物」，皆一義，「貞固」獨二義，何歟？蓋凡屬北方者皆二，亦自然之理爾。噫！人之知，即天之貞。知仁交接，貞下起元，非二義不足以盡之，此又學《易》者之所當知。

「是以立天之道曰陰與陽，立地之道曰柔與剛，立人之道曰仁與義。兼三才而兩之，故《易》六畫而成卦。」
王璠
同考試官學正閻批：《易》卷五百有餘，作此題者主見不一，令人厭觀。此作體認明而措詞健，故表而出之。
translation_en:
…spiritual intelligence [of the human mind], none lacks knowledge, and among all affairs in the world, none lacks principle. Only when one knows the correctness of a principle yet cannot hold fast to it do one's affairs have nothing to rely upon in order to be established. The superior man knows that this is so; once he has the means to know it, he must have the means to hold fast to it. For example, serving one's parents is the affair, while benevolence (ren) is its correct principle; when the superior man truly knows this and holds firmly to it without losing it, the affair of serving parents relies upon it and is established. Obeying one's elder brother is the affair, while righteousness (yi) is its correct principle; when the superior man clearly perceives this and clings steadfastly to it without wavering, the affair of obeying one's elder brother relies upon it and is established. Extending this to all affairs in the world, there is none that is not thus. Who could say that what affairs rely upon to be established does not lie in being correct and firm (zhenggu)? In elucidating wisdom (zhi) in human affairs, the Sage has left nothing further unsaid here. Someone might doubt why, in this passage of the Words of the Text (Wenyan), "embodying benevolence" (ti ren), "beautifying the assemblage" (jia hui), and "benefiting things" (li wu) each consist of a single aspect of meaning, whereas "correct and firm" (zhenggu) alone has two aspects. This is because everything belonging to the North is dual, which is simply a natural principle. Ah! Wisdom in man is precisely correctness/constancy (zheng) in Heaven. Where wisdom and benevolence meet, initiation (yuan) arises beneath constancy (zheng); without two aspects of meaning, it cannot be fully expressed. This, too, is what students of the Book of Changes (Yi) ought to know.

"Therefore, the way of establishing Heaven is called yin and yang; the way of establishing Earth is called the soft and the hard; the way of establishing Man is called benevolence and righteousness. Combining the Three Powers and doubling them, therefore in the Changes six lines form a hexagram."
By Wang Fan 王璠.
Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor (Xuezheng) Yan: There are more than five hundred examination papers on the Book of Changes, and those writing on this topic held disparate central views, making them tiresome to read. This composition shows clear comprehension and vigorous phrasing; therefore I have singled it out for distinction.

Associate Examiner Examining Editor Xing (邢) comments: For this topic from the "Discussion of the Trigrams" (Shuogua), earlier Confucians already have established explanations, yet the candidates write in confused variety without any definite insight. In this essay, both the diction and the reasoning are well-grounded, not comparable to those relying on mere conjecture; therefore, it has been specially selected.

Examiner Vice Minister Ke (柯) comments: The principles of the Book of Changes (Yi) are difficult to elucidate. That this composition is able to convey them in words shows the author must have grasped them in his mind.

Examiner Academician Lü (呂) comments: The writing is concise and the reasoning clear; it accords very well with the purport of the Classic.

When the Sages created the Book of Changes, because the Way of the Three Powers is established in pairs, the lines of the doubled hexagrams were made complete at six. Indeed, the Way cannot be established without duality, and a hexagram cannot be complete without being doubled. When the Sages lodged the Three Powers in the hexagrams and doubled their lines, how supreme was their achievement in creating the Book of Changes! Let us consider this: That which arches high above is Heaven. The Way of Heaven has not only yin, but also yang—such as the alternation of cold and heat. As yin and yang form images, the Way of Heaven is established through duality. That which lies massive below is Earth. The Way of Earth has not only the yielding, but also the firm—such as the flowing of rivers and the towering of mountains. As the firm and the yielding form substance, the Way of Earth is established through duality. That which dwells small in the middle is Man. The Way of Man has not only benevolence, but also righteousness—such as serving one's parents and obeying one's elder brothers. As benevolence and righteousness form virtue, the Way of Man is established through duality. Because the Way of each of the Three Powers is established through duality, when the Sages created the Book of Changes, they did not merely draw trigrams of three lines to embody the Way of the Three Powers, but necessarily combined and doubled them, arriving at six lines. Therefore, combining the Way of Heaven and doubling it, the top line is the yin of Heaven and the fifth line is the yang of Heaven, and thus the Way of Heaven is provided for; combining the Way of Earth [and doubling] it, the second line is the yielding of Earth and the first line is the firm of Earth, and thus the Way of Earth is complete; combining [the Way of] Man…

… the Way of [Humanity] and doubles it: the third line represents the benevolence of humanity, and the fourth line represents the righteousness of humanity, and thus the Way of Humanity is complete. When the three [Powers] are combined, the pairs are whole; when the pairs are whole, the six lines are present. Is this not why the Book of Changes (Yi) is vast, great, and completely equipped? At the beginning of this chapter of the "Discussion of the Trigrams" (Shuogua), it says that when the sages created the Changes, they accorded with the principles of human nature and destiny. The principles of human nature and destiny are none other than yin and yang, the soft and the hard, and benevolence and righteousness. Humans carry yin and yang in order to have life, resemble the soft and the hard in order to take bodily form, and possess benevolence and righteousness as their inner nature. If one can follow one's nature of benevolence and righteousness, then the principles of human nature and destiny will all be gathered within one's own person. Let those who study the Changes strive for this!

Book of Documents (Shu)

"Offices do not go to personal favorites, but only to the capable; ranks of nobility do not go to those of evil virtue, but only to the worthy. Consider what is good before acting, and act only at the proper time."

位不輕授，而惟欲得其人；事不妄行，而尤欲當其可。此大臣告君憲天聰明之道也。夫用人、處事，皆君道所當然；苟位輕授而事妄行，則豈能憲天之聰明哉？昔傅說告高宗之意，若曰：天之聰明，公而已矣。人君欲憲天聰明，可不公於用人、處事哉？是故六卿、百執事，官也；公、卿、大夫、士，爵也。論定而官之，所與共天職，苟及私昵，則非天命之公矣；任官而爵之，所與共天位，苟及惡德，又豈天命之公乎？故官不及於私昵，惟能而有才者則官之，使能者在職，而不才者不得以倖進；爵不及於惡德，惟賢而有德者則爵之，使賢者在位，而不肖者不得以苟容。如是，則位不輕授，而用人合乎天命之公矣。若夫當乎理之謂善，當其可之謂時。事有善與未善也，不先事而慮乎善，則違於天理之公矣；時有宜與未宜也，事雖善而動非時，又寧不違於天理之公乎？故於事未動之先，必極深研幾，熟思審處，以求當乎理而後動；及於事將動之際，又

Comment by Examiner Academician Lü: [Essays whose point is clear and wording concise like this one are rare indeed; I concur with the initial evaluation.]

Positions are not lightly conferred, as one desires only to obtain the right men; affairs are not recklessly carried out, as one especially desires to match what is opportune. This is the Way by which a great minister counsels his sovereign on taking Heaven's intelligence as his model. Now employing men and handling affairs are both what is proper to the Way of a sovereign; if positions are lightly conferred and affairs recklessly carried out, how could one take Heaven's intelligence as a model? Of old, the purport of Fu Yue's counsel to Gaozong was as if to say: Heaven's intelligence is nothing other than impartiality. If a ruler of men wishes to take Heaven's intelligence as his model, how could he not be impartial in employing men and handling affairs? Therefore, the Six Ministers and the hundred executive officers are offices; duke, minister, grand master, and serviceman are ranks of nobility. When one appoints men to office after deliberation is settled, those are the ones with whom one shares Heaven's duties—if this extends to private favorites, it is not the impartiality of Heaven's mandate. When one confers rank upon those who have served in office, those are the ones with whom one shares Heaven's positions—if this extends to men of evil virtue, how again could that be the impartiality of Heaven's mandate? Therefore, offices do not extend to private favorites, and only the capable and talented are appointed to office, so that the capable hold office and the untalented cannot advance by luck; ranks do not extend to men of evil virtue, and only the worthy and virtuous are conferred rank, so that the worthy occupy positions and the unworthy cannot get by through mere accommodation. When it is like this, positions are not lightly conferred, and the employment of men accords with the impartiality of Heaven's mandate. As for what matches principle, it is called goodness; what matches the opportune, it is called timeliness. Affairs may be good or not yet good; if before an affair one does not deliberate on what is good, one violates the impartiality of Heavenly principle. Times may be suitable or not yet suitable; even if an affair is good, if one acts out of time, how does that not also violate the impartiality of Heavenly principle? Therefore, before an affair is set in motion, one must plumb the depths and investigate the subtle springs of action, thinking thoroughly and deliberating carefully in order to seek what matches principle before acting; and when an affair is about to be set in motion, one further…

title: 天順四年會試錄
text:
必因時制宜隨時處中以求當其可而後行如是則
事不妄行而處事合乎天理之公矣吁用人以天而
不以人則聰明見於用人處事以天而不以人則聰
明見於處事然則人君欲憲天聰明者其可不務於
此哉宜傅說惓惓為高宗告也雖然人不足與適也
政不足與間也惟大人為能格君心之非故傅說於
下文又曰惟厥攸居政事惟醇其善於格君者歟

translation_en:
…he must also adapt to the times to determine what is appropriate, and abide in the mean in accordance with the moment, seeking to match what is opportune before acting. If he does so, affairs will not be carried out recklessly, and his handling of affairs will accord with the impartiality of Heavenly Principle. Alas! When one employs men by way of Heaven and not by way of man, then intelligence and perspicacity are manifest in the employment of men; when one handles affairs by way of Heaven and not by way of man, then intelligence and perspicacity are manifest in the handling of affairs. This being so, if a ruler wishes to take Heaven's intelligence and perspicacity as his model, how could he not devote himself to this? Fitting indeed it was that Fu Yue earnestly admonished Gaozong with these words! Even so, "the men he employs are not worth finding fault with, and the governance he conducts is not worth criticizing; only the great man can rectify the errors in the ruler's heart." Therefore, in the passage that follows, Fu Yue further says: "Only in that wherein you abide will your affairs of government be pure." How skilled he was at rectifying his ruler!

"The King was in the new city. He performed the winter sacrifice for the year: to King Wen, one red bull; to King Wu, one red bull. The King commanded that a brevet be made, and Yi recited the prayer on the brevet, announcing solely that the Duke of Zhou would remain behind."

Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, Acting Vice Director: Most writers were unable to elucidate the meaning of using a single victim and making the announcement solely about the Duke of Zhou. This essay has grasped it; the author must be someone thoroughly versed in the Classic, and it ought to be selected for inclusion.
Comment by Associate Examiner Yin, Historiographer: In the examination hall, those writing on this topic mostly used inelegant diction. This essay is classical, regular, and admirable—truly the work of a skilled writer.
Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Historiographer: The topic is originally the historian-official's record of King Cheng retaining the Duke of Zhou to govern Luo and performing the sacrifice and prayer of announcement. On the points of the grand ritual and the weighty affair, most writers were bogged down and failed to express them clearly. Only this essay is vastly different from the crowd's compositions; reading it inspires respect.
Comment by Examiner Ke, Vice Minister: It sets forth the meaning of announcing the retention of the Duke of Zhou very aptly; set it aside for special consideration to await…

title: 天順四年會試錄
text:
考試官學士呂批發明成王留周公之意他卷所無必熟於經者
賢王在新都因時以致享先王者其禮盛作冊以告留
大臣者其事專夫命大臣留後於洛重事也賢王安
得不舉用特盛禮而專告其事於先王哉史臣記於
洛誥篇末者如此思昔成王欲留周公於洛而自歸
於周故在新邑當冬烝之時行歲舉之祭意謂丕顯
文王祀以太牢固宗廟之禮也今命周公留後非盛
其禮可乎於是以騂牛一而祀乎文王焉丕承武王
祭以犧牲亦時享之常也今命周公治洛非異於
===
常可乎於是亦以騂牛一而祀乎武王焉牛用騂者
周尚赤故也然既舉祭祀之禮其可無祝告之冊乎
斯時也成王以作冊為命史佚以祝冊為職意謂成
王嘗命周公監我士師工誕保文武受民矣故冊書
所載惟以周公迪將其後之意達於先王而無他意
焉周公嘗許成王承保乃文祖受命民越乃光烈考
武王矣故祝詞所及惟以周公留守其後之事告於
先王而無餘事焉告曰惟者重留公故也吁時享先
王而必舉夫用特之禮冊告先王而惟載夫留臣之

考試官學士呂批：發明成王留周公之意，他卷所無，必熟於經者。

賢王在新都，因時以致享先王者，其禮盛；作冊以告留大臣者，其事專。夫命大臣留後於洛，重事也；賢王安得不舉用特盛禮，而專告其事於先王哉？史臣記於《洛誥》篇末者如此。思昔成王欲留周公於洛，而自歸於周，故在新邑當冬烝之時，行歲舉之祭。意謂丕顯文王，祀以太牢，固宗廟之禮也；今命周公留後，非盛其禮可乎？於是以騂牛一而祀乎文王焉。丕承武王，祭以犧牲，亦時享之常也；今命周公治洛，非異於常可乎？於是亦以騂牛一而祀乎武王焉。牛用騂者，周尚赤故也。然既舉祭祀之禮，其可無祝告之冊乎？斯時也，成王以作冊為命，史佚以祝冊為職。意謂成王嘗命周公「監我士師工，誕保文武受民」矣，故冊書所載，惟以周公迪將其後之意達於先王，而無他意焉。周公嘗許成王「承保乃文祖受命民，越乃光烈考武王」矣，故祝詞所及，惟以周公留守其後之事告於先王，而無餘事焉。告曰「惟」者，重留公故也。吁！時享先王，而必舉夫用特之禮；冊告先王，而惟載夫留臣之
translation_en:
Comment by Examiner and Academician Lü: This brings out the meaning behind King Cheng keeping the Duke of Zhou behind—something found in no other paper. The author must be thoroughly versed in the Classics.

When the worthy king was in the new capital and took the occasion of the season to offer sacrifice to the former kings, his rites were grand; when he had tablets prepared to announce that he was keeping his great minister behind, his focus was singular. Now, commanding a great minister to remain behind in charge at Luo was a weighty affair; how could the worthy king not perform the grand rite of using a single bull and solely announce this matter to the former kings? Such is what the historian recorded at the end of the "Announcement at Luo" (Luo gao).

Reflecting on the past, King Cheng wished to keep the Duke of Zhou behind at Luo while returning to Zhou himself; therefore, in the new city, at the time of the winter sacrifice (zheng), he performed the annual sacrifice. His thought was that for the illustriously manifest King Wen, sacrificing with the Great牢 (tailao, trio of bull, ram, and boar) was indeed the standard rite of the ancestral temple; yet now, in commanding the Duke of Zhou to remain behind in charge, how could it do not to make the rite especially grand? Thereupon, he sacrificed to King Wen with a single red bull. For the grandly succeeding King Wu, sacrificing with sacrificial victims was likewise the norm of seasonal offerings; yet now, in commanding the Duke of Zhou to govern Luo, how could it do not to make it extraordinary? Thereupon, he likewise sacrificed to King Wu with a single red bull. That red bulls were used is because the Zhou esteemed red.

Yet once the rites of sacrifice were performed, how could there be no inscribed tablets of invocation and announcement? At this time, King Cheng issued the command to prepare the tablets, and Scribal Historian Yi (Shi Yi) performed the duty of reading the invocation tablets. The thought was that King Cheng had previously commanded the Duke of Zhou to "oversee all my officers, instructors, and artisans, and grandly protect the people whom King Wen and King Wu received"; therefore, what was recorded on the tablets conveyed to the former kings solely the intention that the Duke of Zhou should guide and sustain the administration left behind, with no other purpose. The Duke of Zhou had previously promised King Cheng to "uphold and protect the people received by the mandate of your cultured ancestor, and glorify your illustriously meritorious father King Wu"; therefore, what the words of invocation touched upon announced to the former kings solely the matter of the Duke of Zhou remaining behind to guard the administration, with no other affair. That the announcement says "solely" (wei) is because of the gravity of keeping the Duke behind.

Ah! In making the seasonal offering to the former kings, he unfailingly performed the rite of using a single bull; in announcing via inscribed tablets to the former kings, he recorded solely the [matter] of keeping his minister behind…

text:
事成王之慎重也如此哉大抵洛邑之作周公本欲
成王遷都以宅天下之中而成王之意則未欲捨鎬
京而廢祖宗之舊故欲歸周而留周公於後史氏於
洛誥旣以留公祭祀冊告之事附之篇末而又繼之
曰惟周公誕保文武受命惟七年以見留洛之始終
其善於記載也歟

豐水有芑武王豈不仕詒厥孫謀以燕翼子武

事，成王之慎重也如此哉！大抵洛邑之作，周公本欲成王遷都以宅天下之中；而成王之意，則未欲捨鎬京而廢祖宗之舊，故欲歸周而留周公於後。史氏於《洛誥》，旣以留公祭祀冊告之事附之篇末，而又繼之曰：「惟周公誕保文武受命，惟七年。」以見留洛之始終，其善於記載也歟！

《詩》：「豐水有芑，武王豈不仕？詒厥孫謀，以燕翼子。武王烝哉！」

王震
同考試官員外郎程批：遷都、建學、作邑居，乃武王詒謀之事，作者多得此失彼。是篇事旣備而辭不浮，用錄以示後學。

translation_en:
… the matter [of retaining his minister]—how prudent indeed was King Cheng! Broadly speaking, in the building of the city of Luo, the Duke of Zhou originally wished for King Cheng to move the capital so as to reside at the center of the realm; yet King Cheng’s intention was that he did not yet wish to abandon the capital at Hao and discard the old ways of his ancestors, and therefore he wished to return to Zhou while leaving the Duke of Zhou behind. In the "Announcement Concerning Luo" (Luo gao), the Grand Scribe, having appended the matter of retaining the Duke, offering sacrifices, and announcing it by inscribed tablet to the end of the chapter, further continued by saying, "The Duke of Zhou greatly protected the mandate received by King Wen and King Wu for seven years," so as to show the beginning and end of his stay at Luo. How skillful indeed was he at recording events!

Classic of Poetry (Shi): "By the Feng River there is white millet; how could King Wu not have had his work? He bequeathed his plans to his grandsons, to give peace and support to his sons. Truly a sovereign was King Wu!"

Wang Zhen 王震
Comment by Associate Examiner Vice Director Cheng: Moving the capital, establishing the school, and building the royal city for residence are the matters of King Wu’s bequeathed plans; most writers grasp one of these while losing sight of another. In this essay, the facts are complete and the diction is not superficial; it is therefore recorded to serve as a model for future students.
Comment by Associate Examiner Director He: Among no fewer than a thousand papers on the Classic of Poetry, of those writing on this topic who were able to base their argument on the preceding three stanzas, none surpassed this essay.
Comment by Associate Examiner Senior Compiler Chen: Those who write on this topic mostly lack grounding; one that is able to state the actual facts while also employing graceful and smooth phrasing is achieved in this piece.
Comment by Examiner Vice Minister Ke: In composing an exposition on the Odes (Ya), one values broadening its scope; this essay has indeed grasped the teachings of Master Zhu [Zhu Xi 朱熹].
Comment by Examiner Academician Lü: Its argument is rooted in the teachings of Master Zhu and excels at elaborating upon them; it truly deserves to be selected.

title: 天順四年會試錄
text:
詩人托興言聖人遺謀之遠而深美其君道之盡也
盖謀貴乎遠此聖人所以遷鎬也即遷鎬之事而知
遺謀之遠宜詩人托物為興而深美其克君也與昔
詩人言武王遷鎬之事而托興於豐水有芑何耶盖
豐水潤澤而芑之生以蕃土地肥美而芑之生以盛
夫以豐水猶有芑武王豈無所事乎鎬京辟雝此武
王遷都建學之事也事於遷都建學以隆億萬年之
業則謀及其孫也大矣宅是鎬京此武王營度邑居
之事也事於營度邑居以立千百世之傳則謀及其
===
孫也遠矣然謀及其孫則嗣服之成王不頼以為安
哉故夫伴奐爾游而無事於締造之勞者是孰為之
乃武王詒謀之所為也優游爾休而無事於念慮之
勤者是孰致之乃武王詒謀之所致也武王之事如
此信乎能盡君道而為天下後世所共稱也與抑觀
文王遷豐武王遷鎬事同而迹同也而詩人於文王
則曰聿追來孝於武王則曰詒厥孫謀豈其志之異
耶盖致孝所以為詒謀之本而詒謀正所以紹前人
之休也父子一心文武一道周之德於乎隆矣

乃武王詒謀之所爲也優□□爾休而無事於念慮之
勤者是孰致之乃武王詒□□之所致也武王之事如
此信乎能盡君道而爲天□□後世所共稱也與抑觀
文王遷豐武王遷鎬事同□而迹同也而詩人於文王
則曰聿追來孝於武王則□□詒厥孫謀豈其志之異
那盖致孝所以爲詒謀之□□而詒謀正所以紹前人
之休也父子一心文武一□□周之德於乎隆矣
punctuated:
詩人托興言聖人遺謀之遠，而深美其君道之盡也。盖謀貴乎遠，此聖人所以遷鎬也。即遷鎬之事，而知遺謀之遠，宜詩人托物為興，而深美其克君也與！

昔詩人言武王遷鎬之事，而托興於「豐水有芑」，何耶？盖豐水潤澤而芑之生以蕃，土地肥美而芑之生以盛。夫以豐水猶有芑，武王豈無所事乎？「鎬京辟雝」，此武王遷都建學之事也。事於遷都建學，以隆億萬年之業，則謀及其孫也大矣。「宅是鎬京」，此武王營度邑居之事也。事於營度邑居，以立千百世之傳，則謀及其孫也遠矣。然謀及其孫，則嗣服之成王，不頼以為安哉？故夫伴奐爾游，而無事於締造之勞者，是孰為之？乃武王詒謀之所為也。優游爾休，而無事於念慮之勤者，是孰致之？乃武王詒謀之所致也。武王之事如此，信乎能盡君道，而為天下後世所共稱也與！

抑觀文王遷豐、武王遷鎬，事同而迹同也。而詩人於文王則曰「聿追來孝」，於武王則曰「詒厥孫謀」，豈其志之異耶？盖致孝所以為詒謀之本，而詒謀正所以紹前人之休也。父子一心，文武一道，周之德於乎隆矣！
translation_en:
The poet employs an evocative image to speak of the far-reaching nature of the sage’s bequeathed plans, and deeply praises his fulfillment of the way of the ruler. For in planning, what is valued is farsightedness, and this is why the sage moved the capital to Hao. Examining the matter of moving the capital to Hao and thereby recognizing how far-reaching his bequeathed plans were, is it not fitting that the poet takes a natural object as his evocative image and deeply praises him for truly fulfilling the role of ruler?

When the poet of old spoke of King Wu’s moving the capital to Hao, why did he begin with the evocative image of “The Feng River has white millet”? Because when the Feng River moistens and nourishes the land, the growth of white millet becomes luxuriant; when the soil is fertile and rich, the growth of white millet becomes abundant. Now if even the Feng River yields white millet, how could King Wu have had no undertaking of his own? “In the capital of Hao, with its Circular Moat”—this refers to King Wu’s undertaking of moving the capital and establishing the royal college. By devoting himself to moving the capital and establishing the college so as to exalt an enterprise for hundreds of millions of years, his planning that reached down to his grandsons was great indeed! “Taking up residence in this capital of Hao”—this refers to King Wu’s undertaking of laying out and building the capital settlement. By devoting himself to laying out and building the settlement so as to establish a heritage for a百 or a thousand generations, his planning that reached down to his grandsons was far-reaching indeed! And since his plans reached down to his grandsons, did not King Cheng, who succeeded to the royal task, rely upon them for his peace and security? Therefore, wandering about in relaxed leisure, without having to engage in the toil of founding and constructing—who brought this about? It was brought about by the plans bequeathed by King Wu. Resting in unhurried ease, without having to engage in the exertion of anxious thought—who achieved this? It was achieved by the plans bequeathed by King Wu. With King Wu’s undertakings being such as this, truly he was able to fulfill the way of the ruler, and is praised by all the world and later generations alike!

Yet if we observe King Wen’s moving to Feng and King Wu’s moving to Hao, their undertakings were the same and their outward traces were the same. Why then did the poet say of King Wen, “He pursued and carried forward the filial piety that had come down to him,” whereas of King Wu he said, “He bequeathed his plans to his grandsons”? Could it be that their intentions differed? In truth, fulfilling filial piety is the root of bequeathing plans to posterity, and bequeathing plans to posterity is precisely the means of continuing the blessings of one’s predecessors. Father and son were of one mind; King Wen and King Wu shared a single Way. How lofty indeed was the virtue of Zhou!

title: 天順四年會試錄
text:
不僭不濫不敢怠遑
張元禎
同考試官員外郎程批能以朱子本註融會成文
當是作者
同考試官郎中何批此題作者多不知謹刑賞為敬
天畏民之實而於不敢怠遑一句又不知就謹刑賞上説
惟此作得旨非用心於經學者能之乎
同考試官修撰陳批題有關鍵作者漫不知省而忽
易之此篇既能體貼而詞語舂容音響清越若可被之管
絃者可謂善説詩矣
===
考試官少卿柯批此作語和而莊義寛而密頌之意正
如此
考試官學士吕批經義温潤縝密得作詩者之意
觀賢君既公刑賞之事而尤致戒謹之心也盖刑賞
君之奉乎天者也公於民而不私謹於心而不怠此
賢君所以受命中興而為詩人之所頌美也與是詩
説者以為祀高宗之樂也思昔高宗為中興之賢君
而所以敬天畏民者果何如耶亦惟公於刑賞而已

觀賢君既公刑賞之事，而尤致戒謹之心也。盖刑賞，君之奉乎天者也。公於民而不私，謹於心而不怠，此賢君所以受命中興，而為詩人之所頌美也與！是詩，説者以為祀高宗之樂也。思昔高宗為中興之賢君，而所以敬天畏民者果何如耶？亦惟公於刑賞而已。
translation_en:
"Without僭 (overstepping in rewards) and without 濫 (excess in punishments), he did not dare to be indolent or negligent." [Book of Odes, "Yin Wu" 殷武]
Zhang Yuanzhen 張元禎

Comment by Associate Examiner Vice Director Cheng 程: He is able to thoroughly assimilate Master Zhu's [Zhu Xi 朱熹] original commentary into his essay; he is truly a capable writer.
Comment by Associate Examiner Director He 何: Most writers on this topic fail to realize that prudence in punishments and rewards is the actual substance of revering Heaven and standing in awe of the people, and regarding the line "he did not dare to be indolent or negligent," they also fail to explain it in terms of prudence in punishments and rewards. Only this essay grasps the main point—could anyone who has not devoted his mind to classical learning achieve this?
Comment by Associate Examiner Senior Compiler Chen 陳: The topic has a pivotal point that writers casually fail to examine and carelessly overlook. This piece not only closely enters into the meaning, but its diction is unhurried and dignified, and its cadence clear and resonant, as though it could be set to pipes and strings; he may truly be called skillful at explaining the Odes.
Comment by Examiner Vice Minister Ke 柯: In this essay the language is harmonious yet solemn, and the meaning is broad yet closely knit; the spirit of the Hymns (Song 頌) is precisely like this.
Comment by Examiner Academician Lü 呂: This classical explication is warm, lustrous, and finely textured, capturing the intention of the poet.

We observe how the worthy ruler was not only impartial in the matter of punishments and rewards, but even more so maintained to the utmost a cautious and reverent mind. For punishments and rewards are what the ruler administers on behalf of Heaven. Being impartial toward the people without selfish bias, and being cautious in mind without indolence—was this not how the worthy ruler received the Mandate for dynastic revival and came to be eulogized by the poet? Commentators consider this ode to be music for the sacrifice to Gaozong 高宗 [King Wuding 武丁 of Yin]. When we reflect on how in antiquity Gaozong was a worthy ruler of dynastic revival, what indeed was the way by which he revered Heaven and stood in awe of the people? It lay simply in being impartial in punishments and rewards. …

title: 天順四年會試錄
text:
蓋賞所以勸善也賞而或僭則咈民心非敬天矣於
焉賞所當賞賞一人而使千萬人以為慶也刑所以
罰惡也刑而或濫則違民意非敬天矣於焉刑所當
刑刑一人而使千萬人以為威也然今日之賞雖不僭矣使
此心一有怠遑則後日之賞安知不以私喜而或僭
乎故戒懼之心常存於賞善之間始焉如是終焉如
是而賞不移於私喜也今日之刑雖不濫矣使此心
一有荒寧則後日之刑安知不以私怒而或濫乎故
寅畏之念常形於罰惡之時暫焉如是久焉如是而
===
刑不移於私怒也此高宗之敬天畏民久而不替其
受命而中興也宜矣抑觀書稱成湯有曰迪畏天顯
小民又曰推亡固存則成湯之敬天畏民而致謹於
刑賞者至矣而此詩言高宗之事蓋即繼𨗳祖成湯
之心而為之也成湯以是心締造於前高宗以是心
中興於後商業之隆其有以哉
春秋
公觀魚于棠〔隱公五年〕公如齊觀社〔莊公二十三年〕齊人救
邢〔閔公元年〕公會晉侯宋公衛侯曹伯莒子邾子滕

爲賞所當賞賞一人而使千萬人以爲慶也刑所以
罰惡也刑而或濫則違民意非敬天矣於爲刑所當

邢〔閔公元年〕公會晉侯宋公衛侯曹伯莒子邾子滕
punctuated:
蓋賞所以勸善也，賞而或僭，則咈民心，非敬天矣。於焉賞所當賞，賞一人而使千萬人以為慶也。刑所以罰惡也，刑而或濫，則違民意，非敬天矣。於焉刑所當刑，刑一人而使千萬人以為威也。然今日之賞雖不僭矣，使此心一有怠遑，則後日之賞安知不以私喜而或僭乎？故戒懼之心常存於賞善之間，始焉如是，終焉如是，而賞不移於私喜也。今日之刑雖不濫矣，使此心一有荒寧，則後日之刑安知不以私怒而或濫乎？故寅畏之念常形於罰惡之時，暫焉如是，久焉如是，而刑不移於私怒也。此高宗之敬天畏民，久而不替，其受命而中興也宜矣。抑觀《書》稱成湯有曰：「迪畏天顯小民。」又曰：「推亡固存。」則成湯之敬天畏民而致謹於刑賞者至矣。而此詩言高宗之事，蓋即繼𨗳祖成湯之心而為之也。成湯以是心締造於前，高宗以是心中興於後，商業之隆，其有以哉！
《春秋》
公觀魚于棠〔隱公五年〕；公如齊觀社〔莊公二十三年〕；齊人救邢〔閔公元年〕；公會晉侯、宋公、衛侯、曹伯、莒子、邾子、滕
translation_en:
For rewards are the means to encourage goodness; if rewards are ever excessive, they go against the hearts of the people, and this is not revering Heaven. Therefore, he rewarded those who ought to be rewarded, rewarding one person so as to make tens of millions rejoice. Punishments are the means to penalize evil; if punishments are ever abusive, they violate the will of the people, and this is not revering Heaven. Therefore, he punished those who ought to be punished, punishing one person so as to make tens of millions stand in awe. Yet even though today's rewards are not excessive, if this mind once becomes lax and idle, how can one know that future rewards will not become excessive out of private pleasure? Thus, a cautious and fearful mind was always preserved while rewarding the good—being so at the beginning and being so at the end—so that rewards were not swayed by private pleasure. Even though today's punishments are not abusive, if this mind once becomes neglectful and complacent, how can one know that future punishments will not become abusive out of private anger? Thus, a reverent and fearful thought always manifested when penalizing evil—being so for a moment and being so for a long time—so that punishments were not swayed by private anger. That Gaozong revered Heaven and stood in awe of the people for so long without flagging makes it fitting indeed that he received the Mandate and achieved a restoration! Moreover, looking at how the Book of Documents (Shu) praises Cheng Tang, it says, "He walked inreverent awe of Heaven's manifest way and of the common people," and also says, "Overthrow the perishing and strengthen the surviving." Thus Cheng Tang's revering Heaven, standing in awe of the people, and exercising the utmost caution in punishments and rewards were supreme. And when this ode speaks of the deeds of Gaozong, he did them precisely by inheriting and following the mind of his ancestor Cheng Tang. With this mind Cheng Tang founded the dynasty in former times, and with this mind Gaozong achieved a restoration in later times—how well-founded was the flourishing of the Shang enterprise!

Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)

"The Duke watched the fishing at Tang" [Fifth year of Duke Yin]; "The Duke went to Qi to watch the sacrifices at the altar of the soil" [Twenty-third year of Duke Zhuang]; "The men of Qi rescued Xing" [First year of Duke Min]; "The Duke met the Marquis of Jin, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Cao, the Viscount of Ju, the Viscount of Zhu, the Viscount of Teng…"

子、薛伯、杞伯、小邾子、齊世子光伐鄭，同盟于戲。〔襄公九年〕
汪諧
同考試官給事中王批：此篇以禮義立說，引據切當，超於眾作，宜表出之。
同考試官修撰劉批：此篇論四公拒諫、從諫之得失，文足以達其意。末以納諫之美引歸聖人，非有識者不能到，宜寘前列。
考試官少卿柯批：魯為望國，而隱、莊不能為桓、悼之從三諫，此作為之慨然。
考試官學士吕批：詞精義明，必老於《麟經》者。
愎諫而越於禮者可譏，納諫而勇於義者可予。夫人君莫善於納諫，莫不善於愎諫也。《春秋》備書，而我魯與齊、晋之得失較然矣。何則？非禮不動，守身之常度也，况秉禮之君，安可越於禮乎？今也隱公慢棄國政，將如棠以觀魚；莊公急於圖婚，將如齊以觀社。斯時也，僖伯有「官司之守，非君所及」之言，曹劌進「書而不法，後嗣何觀」之諫，其言忠矣。使二公聽而從之，
translation_en:
…[Viscount of Teng], the Earl of Xue, the Earl of Qi, the Viscount of Little Zhu, and Guang, Heir Apparent of Qi, attacked Zheng, and together made a covenant at Xi. [Ninth year of Duke Xiang]

Wang Xie

Comment by Associate Examiner Supervising Secretary Wang: This essay establishes its argument on the basis of ritual propriety and righteousness. Its citations of evidence are apt and fitting, surpassing the other compositions; it ought to be singled out for distinction.

Comment by Associate Examiner Senior Compiler Liu: This essay discusses the successes and failures of the four dukes in rejecting or following remonstrance, and its prose is fully adequate to convey its meaning. At the end, it traces the virtue of accepting remonstrance back to the Sage—something none without true insight could achieve. It ought to be placed in the front ranks.

Comment by Examiner Vice Minister Ke: Lu was a prestigious state, yet Dukes Yin and Zhuang could not match Dukes Huan [of Qi] and Dao [of Jin] in following [even one of] these three remonstrances [?]. This composition expresses deep regret over this.

Comment by Examiner Academician Lü: The diction is refined and the meaning clear; this must be someone well-seasoned in the Classic of the Unicorn [Spring and Autumn Annals].

Those who stubbornly resist remonstrance and transgress ritual propriety deserve criticism; those who accept remonstrance and are courageous in righteousness deserve praise. Now, for a ruler of men, nothing is better than accepting remonstrance, and nothing is worse than stubbornly resisting remonstrance. The Spring and Autumn Annals records these matters in full, and the successes and failures of our state of Lu as compared with Qi and Jin are made manifestly clear. Why is this so? Not acting contrary to ritual propriety is the constant rule for governing one's person; how much less, then, may a ruler who upholds ritual propriety transgress it? Now, Duke Yin negligently abandoned the governance of the state and was about to go to Tang to watch the fishing; Duke Zhuang, overly eager to arrange a marriage, was about to go to Qi to watch the altar-sacrifice. At those times, Zang Xibo offered the words that "this is the duty of the officials in charge, not something with which the ruler should concern himself," and Cao Gui presented the remonstrance that "if an act is recorded and yet is not in accordance with the model, what will posterity have to observe?" Their words were loyal indeed. Had the two dukes listened and followed them,…

title: 天順四年會試錄
text:
夫奚不可奈何慾心一肆忠諫弗入一則淫于遊觀
流連而忘返一則盛其車服冶容以誨淫二公之舉
動如此其如禮何哉書不云乎改過不吝二公何有
焉若夫見義必為君子之當務也况伯主之賢寧不
勇於義乎今也齊桓目擊邢人之難晉悼親駕伐鄭
之師斯時也管仲有諸夏親暱不可棄也之言知罃
陳脩德息師終必獲鄭之策其謀善矣使二公忽而
不納亦奚足取然而嘉謀入告從善如流一則興師
救邢以從簡書之義一則還師盟鄭而得善勝之道
===
伯主之進退若此豈不合於義哉書不云乎從諫弗
咈二公蓋有焉雖然從諫之益豈特伯者為然神如
堯舜尚置敢諫之鼓立誹謗之木聖如湯武尚納仲
虺之言受尚父之戒而况不及堯舜湯武之萬一者
乎噫此桓悼所以為春秋之賢君而隱莊不與也宜

夫奚不可？奈何慾心一肆，忠諫弗入。一則淫于遊觀，流連而忘返；一則盛其車服，冶容以誨淫。二公之舉動如此，其如禮何哉？《書》不云乎：「改過不吝。」二公何有焉？若夫見義必為，君子之當務也，况伯主之賢，寧不勇於義乎？今也齊桓目擊邢人之難，晉悼親駕伐鄭之師。斯時也，管仲有「諸夏親暱，不可棄也」之言；知罃陳「脩德息師，終必獲鄭」之策，其謀善矣。使二公忽而不納，亦奚足取？然而嘉謀入告，從善如流：一則興師救邢，以從簡書之義；一則還師盟鄭，而得善勝之道。伯主之進退若此，豈不合於義哉？《書》不云乎：「從諫弗咈。」二公蓋有焉。雖然，從諫之益，豈特伯者為然？神如堯、舜，尚置敢諫之鼓，立誹謗之木；聖如湯、武，尚納仲虺之言，受尚父之戒。而况不及堯、舜、湯、武之萬一者乎？噫！此桓、悼所以為《春秋》之賢君，而隱、莊不與也。宜哉！

translation_en:
…what would have been improper? Yet once their selfish desires ran unchecked, loyal remonstrances could find no entry. One indulged excessively in sightseeing, lingering until he forgot to return; the other arrayed his carriages and robes in splendor, adorning his appearance in a manner that invited licentiousness. With the conduct of the two dukes being such as this, what did they care for ritual propriety? Does not the Book of Documents (Shu) say, "Do not be reluctant to correct your faults"? What part of this did the two dukes possess?

As for seeing righteousness and unfailingly acting upon it, that is the proper duty of the gentleman; how much more so for worthy hegemons—how could they not be courageous in righteousness? Now Duke Huan of Qi (Qi Huan) witnessed with his own eyes the distress of the people of Xing, and Duke Dao of Jin (Jin Dao) personally led an army to attack Zheng. At those moments, Guan Zhong spoke the words, "The various Xia states are close kin and must not be abandoned," while Zhi Ying set forth the strategy of "cultivating virtue and resting the troops,whereby we shall surely win over Zheng in the end." Their counsels were admirable indeed. Had the two dukes disregarded and refused to accept them, what would there be in them worthy of praise? Yet when fine counsels were reported within, they followed the good like a flowing stream: the one raised an army to rescue Xing, thereby heeding the righteous duty appealed to in the bamboo dispatches; the other withdrew his troops and covenanted with Zheng, thereby attaining the way of a bloodless victory. With the advances and retreats of the hegemons being such as this, did they not accord with righteousness? Does not the Book of Documents say, "Follow remonstrance without resistance"? The two dukes truly possessed this quality.

Even so, is the benefit of following remonstrance true only for hegemons? Divine as Yao and Shun were, they still set up the drum for bold remonstrance and erected the post for criticisms; sagely as Tang and Wu were, they still accepted the words of Zhonghui and received the admonitions of Shangfu. How much more so for those who do not reach one ten-thousandth of Yao, Shun, Tang, and Wu? Alas! This is why Dukes Huan and Dao were worthy rulers of the Spring and Autumn (Chunqiu) period, whereas Dukes Yin and Zhuang had no part among them. How fitting indeed!

The Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, a man of Jiang, and a man of Huang met at Yanggu [3rd year of Duke Xi]. The Duke met with the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Zheng, the Baron of Xu, and the Earl of Cao to make an incursion into Cai, and thereupon attacked Chu [4th year of Duke Xi]. The Duke met with the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, Heir Apparent Kuan of Chen, and Heir Apparent Hua of Zheng…

Associate Examiner Supervising Secretary Wang comments: This essay discusses how the successes and failures of the deeds of Duke Huan of Qi and Duke Wen of Jin stemmed from the uprightness or craftiness of their minds. Its diction is upright and rigorous; it is truly a masterpiece.

Associate Examiner Senior Compiler Liu comments: The argument is brilliant and vigorous, and the literary vitality is mature. The successes and failures of Duke Huan and Duke Wen are fully revealed at a single glance. In my examination ward, how could many essays like this be found?

Examiner Vice Minister Ke comments: Its praise and blame capture the essential meaning [of the Spring and Autumn Annals], and at the end of the essay it further reproves Duke Huan of Qi—a thought that is exceptionally incisive and striking.

Examiner Academician Lü comments: The argument is sound and proper, and its rising and falling cadences and repeated turns carry lingering meaning that ordinary compositions cannot match.

From the successes and failures of the hegemons' deeds, one sees the uprightness or craftiness of the hegemons' minds. Now, uprightness and craftiness reside in the mind and are manifested in deeds; if one examines their minds on the basis of their deeds, how could the successes and failures of Duke Huan and Duke Wen be concealed? Moreover, among the feudal lords of the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu), the Five Hegemons are praised first, and among the worthies of the Five Hegemons, Duke Huan and Duke Wen are praised first; yet Duke Wen was no match for Duke Huan. How can this be seen? When Duke Huan founded his hegemony, there was the meeting at Yanggu to plan an attack on Chu…

寗母有盟謀服鄭也子華有請疑可納其言矣公則
以其干禮而不納以至葵丘之會不邇三川以王畿
所在也葵丘之盟不加宰孔以王臣當尊也吁啟戎
招寇漸不可長公不肯為也以子奸父義不可訓公
不忍為也况敢逼王畿以瀆王臣哉孔子曰齊桓公

不恤後患而致秦于征衞侯有罪元晅訴也則不顧
大義而聽晅之讒以至翟泉王城之近地乃使大夫

… When Jiang and Huang submitted, it seemed he could have drawn upon their strength, yet the Duke worried that this would pave the way for disorder and did not employ them. At Ningmu there was a covenant to plot the subjugation of Zheng; when Zihua made a request, it seemed his words might be accepted, yet because it offended against ritual propriety, the Duke did not accept it. Furthermore, the assembly at Kuiqiu was not held near the Three Rivers, because the royal domain lay there; and the covenant at Kuiqiu was not imposed upon Royal Steward Kong (Zai Kong), because a minister of the King ought to be revered. Alas! To provoke foreign tribes and invite brigands is a tendency that must not be allowed to grow, and the Duke refused to do it; for a son to transgress against his father is a breach of righteousness that cannot be taught as an example, and the Duke could not bear to do it. How much less would he dare encroach upon the royal domain or show disrespect to a minister of the King! Confucius said: "Duke Huan of Qi was upright and not crafty." Truly so!

When Duke Wen succeeded to the hegemony, there was the battle at Chengpu to check the unbridled arrogance of Chu, yet without regard for future trouble he brought Qin into the campaign. When the Marquis of Wei was at fault and Yuan Xuan brought a complaint against him, without regard for great righteousness he listened to Xuan's slander. Furthermore, although Diquan was a place close to the royal capital, he sent great officers to exact a covenant there; and although Zihu was a noble minister of the royal house, he permitted the ranked ministers of the states to smear their lips with blood alongside him. Alas! That one must not join in enterprises with the Yi and Di barbarians was something Huan refused to do, yet Duke Wen did it; that ruler and subject must not be made opposing parties in a lawsuit was something Huan could not bear to do, yet Duke Wen did it. How much less could one expect him not to crowd the royal domain or coerce a man of the King! Confucius said: "Duke Wen of Jin was crafty and not upright." Fittingly so!

Even so, if we compare Huan with Wen, Huan is certainly superior; yet if we measure him by the Kingly Way, how could Huan's actions have issued entirely from uprightness? That he did not employ Jiang and Huang to attack Chu was acceptable, yet was it acceptable to do so without requesting the King's command? That he did not accept Zihua's request was acceptable, yet was it acceptable to include him in the assembly rankings? Moreover, its diction and tone are warm and generous, allowing one to envision the author's personal character.
Comment by Associate Examiner Historiographer-Compiler Wang 王: Those who write on the “Record of Music” (Yueji) generally offer the explanation that music serves to manifest virtue, without investigating the purport of how the Odes regulate human nature and emotions—limp, listless, and tiresome. This essay perceives the moral principles clearly, and its language is furthermore rich and lustrous. Reading it is like listening to the Airs of the States, the Odes, and the Hymns; one cannot help but admire and praise it.
Comment by Examiner Vice Minister (Shaoqing) Ke 柯: The diction is filled with vital breath while moral principle is equally achieved; truly an extraordinary figure among the candidates coming up for the metropolitan examination.
Comment by Examiner Academician (Xueshi) Lü 呂: It elaborates the purport of how the Odes regulate human nature and emotions, leaving almost nothing unexpressed. Moreover, its diction and tone are unhurried and dignified; none but one thoroughly versed in the Classic could have produced it.

title: 天順四年會試錄
text:
知人之歌詩隨其德而異其宜則知歌之於人正其
身而敷其德盖歌詠以養其性情故有此德者宜此
歌也然則正直其身而敷陳其德又豈有外於歌者
哉今夫人之性情不同詩之興趣亦異故取其興趣
以理其性情者各有所宜焉是故寛裕而安靜和柔
而正直者宜歌夫三頌頌以美盛德取之所以成其
包含之德也弘大而靜深疏通而信實者宜歌夫大
雅雅以陳王政取之所以成其正大之德也陳王政
之小者謂之小雅必持敬而惟禮是好守約而非禮
===
不為者宜歌之以擴充其德量焉繫一國之事者謂
之風必正直而不躁妄廉介而不矜持者宜歌之以
涵養其德性焉商者五帝之遺聲也其音剛決故宜
德之寛舒而徑直慈惠而仁愛者歌之則有以變其
柔而為剛斷矣齊者三代之遺聲也其音柔緩故宜
德之和厚而易直剛果而能斷者歌之則有以變其
剛而為柔遜矣惟其有此德而宜此歌則歌之為言
豈徒長言之而已哉所以正直其身使不至於偏倚
而為中正之歸敷陳其德使不昧於隱微而極發揚

punctuated: 知人之歌詩，隨其德而異其宜，則知歌之於人，正其身而敷其德。盖歌詠以養其性情，故有此德者宜此歌也。然則正直其身而敷陳其德，又豈有外於歌者哉？今夫人之性情不同，詩之興趣亦異，故取其興趣以理其性情者，各有所宜焉。是故寛裕而安靜、和柔而正直者，宜歌夫《三頌》。《頌》以美盛德，取之所以成其包含之德也。弘大而靜深、疏通而信實者，宜歌夫《大雅》。《雅》以陳王政，取之所以成其正大之德也。陳王政之小者謂之《小雅》，必持敬而惟禮是好、守約而非禮不為者宜歌之，以擴充其德量焉。繫一國之事者謂之《風》，必正直而不躁妄、廉介而不矜持者宜歌之，以涵養其德性焉。《商》者，五帝之遺聲也，其音剛決，故宜德之寛舒而徑直、慈惠而仁愛者歌之，則有以變其柔而為剛斷矣。《齊》者，三代之遺聲也，其音柔緩，故宜德之和厚而易直、剛果而能斷者歌之，則有以變其剛而為柔遜矣。惟其有此德而宜此歌，則歌之為言，豈徒長言之而已哉？所以正直其身，使不至於偏倚，而為中正之歸；敷陳其德，使不昧於隱微，而極發揚
translation_en:
When one understands that the songs a person sings vary in their suitability according to his virtue, one understands that singing, in relation to a person, rectifies his person and spreads forth his virtue. This is because singing and chanting nourish one's nature and emotions; therefore, one who possesses a given virtue is suited to a given song. This being so, how could rectifying one's person and setting forth one's virtue lie outside of singing?

Now, people's natures and emotions differ, and the evocative qualities of the Odes also vary; therefore, in drawing upon their evocative qualities to regulate one's nature and emotions, each person has what is suited to him. Thus, those who are broad-minded and tranquil, gentle yet upright, ought to sing the Three Eulogies (San Song). The Eulogies praise flourishing virtue, and one draws upon them in order to perfect one's all-embracing virtue. Those who are magnanimous and serenely profound, discerning and trustworthy, ought to sing the Major Court Hymns (Da Ya). The Court Hymns set forth kingly governance, and one draws upon them in order to perfect one's upright and great virtue. Those that set forth the lesser matters of kingly governance are called the Minor Court Hymns (Xiao Ya); surely those who maintain reverence and love propriety alone, who abide by restraint and do nothing contrary to propriety, ought to sing them in order to expand the capacity of their virtue. Those tied to the affairs of a single state are called the Airs of the States (Feng); surely those who are upright and not rash, incorruptible and not boastful, ought to sing them in order to nurture their moral nature. The Shang airs are the surviving melodies of the Five Emperors; their tones are firm and decisive. Therefore, it is fitting for those whose virtue is relaxed and straightforward, kind and benevolent, to sing them, so that they have the means to transform their softness into firm decisiveness. The Qi airs are the surviving melodies of the Three Dynasties; their tones are gentle and slow. Therefore, it is fitting for those whose virtue is harmonious and plain, resolute and capable of decision, to sing them, so that they have the means to transform their hardness into gentle humility.

Precisely because having a given virtue makes a given song suitable, how could "singing" (ge) mean merely drawing out the words in a prolonged voice? It is the means by which one rectifies one's person, keeping it from leaning to one side so that it returns to balanced rectitude, and sets forth one's virtue, keeping it from remaining obscured in subtlety so that it reaches the utmost flourishing of manifestation…

translation_en:
…the flourishing of [its] [?]. Such is the benefit of vocal song to humankind! Moreover, if we examine this chapter of the Record of Music (Yueji), Zigong 子贛 asked Music Master Yi 師乙 what kind of songs were fitting for him to sing. Considering himself a lowly musician who dared not presume to answer the question of a worthy, Master Yi asked leave to recite what he had heard and let Zigong choose for himself what to hold to. Since Zigong always possessed self-knowledge, he was surely able to judge carefully what suited him, seek it within the Three Hundred Poems, and grasp its spirit and inspiration so as to nurture his nature and feelings. When on another day the Master praised him as one "with whom one can speak of the Odes," might he not also have gained something from these words?

"Ritual takes human feelings as its basis and makes regulating measures and refinements for them, so as to serve as a dike for the people."
By Chen Xuan 陳選.
Comment by Associate Examiner Historiographer Qiu 丘: Candidates in the examination hall are generally able to write on this topic from the "Record of the Dikes" (Fangji), but one very rarely finds a composition as detailed, well-ordered, and lucidly articulated as this. From beginning to end there is not a superfluous word or a perverse idea—an excellent piece.
Comment by Associate Examiner Historiographer Wang 王: Students of the Rites in recent times mostly prize the strange and abstruse, while sometimes slighting and neglecting what is clear, plain, and essential in the institutions of the former kings. This essay elucidates the meaning of ritual as a safeguard against the people's excesses; both its diction and its reasoning hit the mark. Is it not indeed capable of rectifying their biases and bringing them back to what is orthodox?
Comment by Examiner Vice Minister Ke 柯: The explanation of moral principle is exceedingly clear. It is selected for publication as a warning to those who go against the Rites.
Comment by Examiner Academician Lü 吕: Its grasp of the classic's import is thorough and clear, and its brushwork is mature and vigorous. Expositions of the classics like this are rarely come by; it rightly belongs among the selected essays.

The rituals of the former kings were instituted in accordance with human feelings, and are the means of setting up a great barrier for humankind. For human feelings harbor desires that know no bounds; had the former kings not instituted regulations on the basis of those feelings, then…

text:
將何以防閑之哉今夫禮者天理之節文人事之儀
則也先王之制是禮非徒有是樽節也不過因人情
之有有餘者而品節之爾非徒有是繁文也不過因
人情之有不足者而文飾之爾彼其貧斯約約斯盜
者人之情也禮則因其情而為一夫受田百畝之制
使之不以不足而窮其身焉富斯驕驕斯亂者人之
情也禮則因其情而為家富不過百乘之制使之不
以有餘而慢於人焉防其不足所以止斯民羨慕之
心亦猶隄防遏水之流而不至於奔潰也以此閑民
孰敢過乎制其有餘所以止斯民僭僣之心亦猶隄
防禦水之來而不至於泛溢也以此防民孰敢踰乎
吁厭貧求富者人之情也聖人始因情而為之禮貧
約富驕者情之欲也聖人還以禮而防其情禮之為
用大矣哉抑論先王制禮非止於防民也而坊記一
篇每以坊民為言首章既曰坊民之所不足而以此坊
民之言又屢見於各章之中蓋以民不足於防之之
道故防之設也以民為主若夫君子以禮自防則無
俟乎人為之防矣此又讀禮者之所當知
