punctuated: 將何以防閑之哉？今夫禮者，天理之節文，人事之儀則也。先王之制是禮，非徒有是樽節也，不過因人情之有有餘者而品節之爾；非徒有是繁文也，不過因人情之有不足者而文飾之爾。彼其貧斯約、約斯盜者，人之情也，禮則因其情而為一夫受田百畝之制，使之不以不足而窮其身焉；富斯驕、驕斯亂者，人之情也，禮則因其情而為家富不過百乘之制，使之不以有餘而慢於人焉。防其不足，所以止斯民羨慕之心，亦猶隄防遏水之流而不至於奔潰也，以此閑民，孰敢過乎？制其有餘，所以止斯民僭僣之心，亦猶隄防禦水之來而不至於泛溢也，以此防民，孰敢踰乎？吁！厭貧求富者，人之情也，聖人始因情而為之禮；貧約富驕者，情之欲也，聖人還以禮而防其情。禮之為用大矣哉！抑論先王制禮，非止於防民也，而《坊記》一篇，每以坊民為言。首章既曰「坊民之所不足」，而「以此坊民」之言又屢見於各章之中，蓋以民不足於防之之道，故防之設也以民為主；若夫君子以禮自防，則無俟乎人為之防矣。此又讀《禮》者之所當知。
translation_en: … how else would one keep them within bounds? Now, ritual propriety is the regulated refinement of Heavenly Principle and the standard of conduct for human affairs. When the former kings instituted these rites, it was not merely to impose such restraints for their own sake; it was simply to grade and moderate those areas where human feelings are in excess. Nor was it merely to create such elaborate forms for their own sake; it was simply to adorn and refine those areas where human feelings are deficient. That poverty leads to distress and distress leads to theft is in the nature of human feelings; ritual propriety therefore accommodates these feelings by establishing the system whereby each husbandman receives a hundred mu of land, ensuring that he is not driven to extremity by deficiency. That wealth leads to arrogance and arrogance leads to disorder is also in the nature of human feelings; ritual propriety therefore accommodates these feelings by establishing the system whereby a wealthy noble household does not exceed a hundred chariots, ensuring that it does not treat others with contempt out of excess. Guarding against people's deficiencies serves to check their covetous desires, just as dikes hold back the flow of water so that it does not burst forth in a ruinous flood; when the people are kept within bounds by this means, who would dare go too far? Regulating their excesses serves to check their presumptuous ambitions, just as dikes resist the onrush of water so that it does not overflow; when the people are restrained by this means, who would dare transgress? Ah! To loathe poverty and seek wealth is in the nature of human feelings, and the sages at first instituted ritual propriety in accordance with those feelings; yet to become distressed in poverty and arrogant in wealth comes from the desires of those feelings, and so the sages in turn used ritual propriety to guard against them. Great indeed is the function of ritual propriety! Moreover, if we consider the former kings' institution of ritual propriety, it was not limited to restraining the common people; yet the "Record of the Dykes" (Fangji) chapter repeatedly speaks in terms of dyking the people. Its opening section states, "dyking the people where they are deficient," and the phrase "by this means dyking the people" appears time and again throughout its various sections. This is because the common people are deficient in the Way of restraining themselves, and thus the setting up of dykes takes the common people as its primary object; as for the noble man, he restrains himself through ritual propriety and has no need of others to set up restraints for him. This too is something that readers of the Record of Rites (Liji) ought to know.

title: 天順四年會試錄
text:
即天之心乎盖元亨利貞於穆不已天之性也生長
收藏變化無窮天之情也人受天命而生而得其所
以生我者以為心故其體即元亨利貞之道具而為
仁義禮智之性其用即生長收藏之機形而為惻隱
羞惡辭讓是非之情性雖蘊於中而實情之體情雖
發於外而實性之用心則管攝乎體用者也夫豈不
能妙性情之德哉以性而言心之德曰仁心之制曰
義而禮者心之敬智者心之別也是皆渾然在中若
鑑之空若衡之平信乎寂然不動矣而其所以寂然
===
不動者庸非心有以主宰之乎以情而言仁之心為
惻隱義之心為羞惡而辭讓者禮之心是非者智之
心也是皆隨感即應若火之然若泉之達信乎感而
遂通矣而其所以感而遂通者庸非心有以運用之
乎惟心主宰乎仁義禮智之性而運用乎惻隱羞惡
辭讓是非之情由是性雖具於方寸之間而其本然
之體實與天之元亨利貞同其體情雖發乎方寸之
間而其本然之用實與天之生長收藏同其用與天
同體非特妙性之德而已而萬理悉總於一心所謂

punctuated: 即天之心乎？盖元亨利貞，於穆不已，天之性也；生長收藏，變化無窮，天之情也。人受天命而生，而得其所以生我者以為心。故其體即元亨利貞之道，具而為仁義禮智之性；其用即生長收藏之機，形而為惻隱、羞惡、辭讓、是非之情。性雖蘊於中，而實情之體；情雖發於外，而實性之用。心則管攝乎體用者也，夫豈不能妙性情之德哉？以性而言，心之德曰仁，心之制曰義，而禮者心之敬，智者心之別也。是皆渾然在中，若鑑之空，若衡之平，信乎寂然不動矣。而其所以寂然不動者，庸非心有以主宰之乎？以情而言，仁之心為惻隱，義之心為羞惡，而辭讓者禮之心，是非者智之心也。是皆隨感即應，若火之然，若泉之達，信乎感而遂通矣。而其所以感而遂通者，庸非心有以運用之乎？惟心主宰乎仁義禮智之性，而運用乎惻隱、羞惡、辭讓、是非之情，由是性雖具於方寸之間，而其本然之體，實與天之元亨利貞同其體；情雖發乎方寸之間，而其本然之用，實與天之生長收藏同其用。與天同體，非特妙性之德而已，而萬理悉總於一心，所謂
translation_en:
…indeed the mind of Heaven? Now, origination, flourishing, advantage, and firmness, profound and unceasing—these are the nature of Heaven. Birth, growth, harvest, and storage, transforming without end—these are the feelings of Heaven. Humans are born having received the Mandate of Heaven, and obtain that by which they are given life to serve as their mind. Therefore, its substance is none other than the Way of origination, flourishing, advantage, and firmness, which is endowed in us as the nature of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom; its function is none other than the mechanism of birth, growth, harvest, and storage, which takes form as the feelings of commiseration, shame and dislike, deference and compliance, and approval and disapproval. Although the nature is stored within, it is in fact the substance of the feelings; although the feelings issue forth to the outside, they are in fact the function of the nature. The mind, then, is that which governs and integrates both substance and function. How could it fail to wondrously unify the virtues of nature and feelings?

Speaking in terms of the nature: the virtue of the mind is called benevolence, the regulation of the mind is called righteousness, while propriety is the reverence of the mind, and wisdom is the discernment of the mind. All of these are seamlessly complete within, like the emptiness of a mirror or the levelness of a balance—truly, they are tranquil and unmoving! Yet as for why they are tranquil and unmoving, is it not because the mind presides over them? Speaking in terms of the feelings: the mind of benevolence is commiseration, the mind of righteousness is shame and dislike, while deference and compliance are the mind of propriety, and approval and disapproval are the mind of wisdom. All of these respond immediately upon being stirred, like a fire catching flame or a spring bursting forth—truly, when stirred they penetrate everywhere! Yet as for why they penetrate everywhere when stirred, is it not because the mind puts them into operation?

Only because the mind presides over the nature of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom, and puts into operation the feelings of commiseration, shame and dislike, deference and compliance, and approval and disapproval, therefore although the nature is contained within the square inch of the heart, its original substance in fact shares the same substance as Heaven's origination, flourishing, advantage, and firmness; and although the feelings issue forth from within the square inch of the heart, their original function in fact shares the same function as Heaven's birth, growth, harvest, and storage. Sharing the same substance with Heaven, it does not merely bring out the marvel of the virtue of the nature; rather, all the myriad principles are gathered within a single mind, which is what is called…

title: 天順四年會試錄
text:
天下之大本也與天同用非特妙情之德而已而萬
化皆出於一心所謂天下之達道也大本立而達道
行則性情之德極其至所以位天地育萬物者皆不
出乎此心主宰運用之外矣大哉心乎其所以參夫
天地而靈於萬物者乎雖然上自聖人下至衆人其
心一也其性情同也而或有不能妙者何耶蓋聖人
之心純乎天賢人之學幾乎聖是以能妙性情之德
衆人則拘滯於有形而不能通是以或鑿其性汩其情
而莫能妙也然能探視聽言動無息之本以知夫性

則豈有不能妙之者哉所謂士希賢賢希聖聖希天

「天下之大本」也；與天同用，非特妙情之德而已，而萬化皆出於一心，所謂「天下之達道」也。大本立而達道行，則性情之德極其至，所以位天地、育萬物者，皆不出乎此心主宰、運用之外矣。大哉心乎！其所以參夫天地而靈於萬物者乎！雖然，上自聖人，下至衆人，其心一也，其性情同也，而或有不能妙者，何耶？蓋聖人之心純乎天，賢人之學幾乎聖，是以能妙性情之德；衆人則拘滯於有形而不能通，是以或鑿其性、汩其情，而莫能妙也。然能探視聽言動無息之本以知夫性，察視聽言動無息之際以會夫情，而主敬以養其心，則豈有不能妙之者哉？所謂「士希賢，賢希聖，聖希天」者，此也。是為論。

translation_en:
… is called "the great foundation of all under heaven." Sharing the same function as Heaven is not merely a matter of bringing into wondrous play the virtue of the emotions, for the myriad transformations all issue from a single mind—this is what is called "the universal path of all under heaven." When the great foundation is established and the universal path is carried out, the virtue of human nature and the emotions reaches its utmost perfection, and that whereby Heaven and Earth are given their proper places and the myriad things are nourished never goes beyond the governance and operation of this mind. Great indeed is the mind! Is it not that whereby man forms a triad with Heaven and Earth and is the most spiritually endowed of the myriad things?

Even so, from the sages above down to the multitude below, their mind is one, and their nature and emotions are the same; why is it, then, that some are unable to bring them into wondrous play? It is because the mind of the sage is purely one with Heaven, and the learning of the worthy comes close to the sage, so that they are able to bring into wondrous play the virtue of nature and the emotions; the multitude, however, are bound and obstructed by physical form and cannot penetrate beyond it, and thus they sometimes mutilate their nature and confound their emotions, and none can bring them into wondrous play. Yet if one can probe the unceasing root of seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting in order to know human nature, examine the unceasing occasions of seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting in order to comprehend the emotions, and maintain reverence so as to nourish the mind, then how could anyone fail to bring them into wondrous play? What is meant by the saying, "The scholar aspires to be a worthy, the worthy aspires to be a sage, and the sage aspires to Heaven," is precisely this. Such is my discourse.

Examiner and Academician Lü comments: The drafted edict is smooth and coherent.

The edict reads: In antiquity, the Xia, Yin, and Zhou dynasties successively established the Three First Months of the Year. Qin did not take antiquity as its teacher and first used the hai month as the first month of the year, and Our dynasty followed this without change. Recently, the Superior Grand Masters of the Palace Gongsun Qing 公孫卿 and Hu Sui 壺遂, the Grand Astrologer Sima Qian 司馬遷, and others have stated that in regulating the calendar and clarifying the seasons, it is imperative first to rectify the first month and first day of the year. When this was handed down to the body of officials for deliberation, all said that it is proper to use the first month of the Xia. Did Confucius not say, "Follow the calendar of the Xia"? This is indeed the great standard for a hundred kings. We specially command Qing, Sui, Qian, and the others jointly to compile the Grand Inception Calendar (Taichu li) and to take the first month as the beginning of the year. Proclaim this to all under Heaven so that all may be made to know it.

translation_en: …and a position to which all eyes look up; filled with the dread of treading on an abyss or thin ice, how can this decayed old frame bear it! This is all because I have humbly encountered [Your Majesty]: sage by Heaven's endowment, and of virtue renewed day by day. Filial, fraternal, modest, and reverent, You are truly a sovereign who appears but once in generations; rousing Your energies to seek good governance, You are genuinely a ruler of great accomplishment. First brings harmony with public sentiment by thoroughly abolishing the New Laws of the former minister; dedicating Yourself to relieving the distress of the people, You gloriously restore the old institutions of the former kings. Worthies and talents fill the court, all pouring out their hearts to assist in the great transformation; songs of praise fill the roads, as all wipe their eyes to behold the era of Great Peace. In the past, during the former reign, Your servant undeservedly received a heavy charge. Long occupying the post of Privy Councilor, I was ashamed of having contributed nothing to the Imperial plan; happening to discuss critical affairs of state, I was suddenly said to be at odds with prevailing opinion. I submitted a memorial begging to be relieved of office, and an edict permitted me to return to my fields. Like a weary bird that knows to return home, I had already resigned myself to ending my days in a ditch; yet the returning phoenix-carriage showed favor, and I repeatedly received the grace of being gathered in like turnips and radishes that are not cast aside for their roots. Reply: In generating living things, Heaven and Earth are most generous to humankind, and the nature that holds fast to the constant norms is the same in all; in generating humankind, Heaven and Earth are most generous to the sages, and the responsibility of upholding the canons of human relationships is weighty. Truly, the people's holding fast to the constant norms and the ruler's upholding of the canons are both nothing outside the Five Constant Virtues; thus their underlying principle is inherently no different. Why, then, must one cling rigidly to the differences in their names and definitions? I beg leave to set this forth in response to the illustrious question.

When human beings are born, they receive the finest essence of the Five Phases and become the most spiritually endowed of the myriad things, and the Way by which they are human lies nowhere outside the Five Constants. Therefore, what is endowed in the mind is simply benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and trustworthiness; what is engaged in through one's person is simply affection between father and son, righteousness between ruler and minister, distinction between husband and wife, precedence between older and younger, and trustworthiness between friends—there is no other Way. Near at hand, that by which one cultivates the person and regulates the family is assuredly this Way; far afield, that by which one governs the state and brings peace to the world is also this Way. One cannot be without it for a single day. How could those who bear responsibility for the Way of the world not regard it as their foremost duty?

punctuated: 之誥；宣宗章皇帝繼體守文，恢弘大化，而於五倫有纂輯之書。以淑斯民於皇極，以措斯世於雍熙，所以為天下計者至矣。以往古言之：唐虞時，堯命舜「愼徽五典」，舜命契「敬敷五教」，其曰「五品不遜」，亦舜告契之言也；商周時，成湯革夏正而「肇脩人紀」，武王政由舊而「重民五教」，其曰「彝倫攸叙」，亦武王訪箕子之辭也。孔子告哀公有曰：「天下之達道五」，其言載於《中庸》之書；孟子論堯舜有曰：「聖人，人倫之至」，其言見於七篇之内。是則堯、舜、湯、武之立教，孔、孟之立言，皆不外乎五常之道矣。是道也，語其常行不易曰五常，語其有序不紊曰五倫。五教云者，以當然之理為教令也，而曰人紀者，非禮義相維之謂乎？彝倫云者，以人倫之道皆常理也，而曰達道者，非古今共由之謂乎？要之，其名雖殊，而其理一也。申明云者，慮有未明，故申而明之；愼徽云者，慮有未美，故謹而美之。敬布其教於民曰敬敷，謂之肇脩，則以
translation_en:
… mandate; and Emperor Xuanzong, the Illustrious (Xuanzong Zhang Huangdi), succeeding to the throne and maintaining the civil order, broadened and magnified the great transformation, and with respect to the Five Human Relationships had a book compiled. Thereby improving the people through the August Ultimate and placing the world in harmonious prosperity, the plans made on behalf of the realm were comprehensive indeed.

Speaking in terms of remote antiquity: in the time of Tang and Yu, Yao commanded Shun to "carefully beautify the five canonical relationships," and Shun commanded Xie to "reverently spread the five teachings"; the phrase "the five classes are not compliant" was also what Shun told Xie. In the time of Shang and Zhou, Cheng Tang reformed the mandate of Xia and "began to cultivate the human綱紀 (bonds of human society)," while King Wu governed according to the old ways and "attached great importance to the people's five teachings"; the phrase "whereby the invariable human relationships are set in order" was also taken from the words of King Wu's inquiry to Jizi. Confucius told Duke Ai, "The universal ways of the world are five," and his words are recorded in the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong); Mencius, in discussing Yao and Shun, said, "The sage is the culmination of human relationships," and his words appear within the Seven Books (of the Mencius). Thus the establishment of teachings by Yao, Shun, Tang, and Wu, and the establishment of words by Confucius and Mencius, all do not go beyond the Way of the Five Constant Virtues.

As for this Way, speaking of its constant practice without change, it is called the Five Constant Virtues (wuchang); speaking of its orderly sequence without confusion, it is called the Five Human Relationships (wulun). What is called the "five teachings" (wujiao) takes the principles of what ought to be as instructional decrees; and when it is called the "bonds of human society" (renji), does this not mean binding people together through ritual propriety and righteousness? What is called the "invariable human relationships" (yilun) means that the ways of human relationships are all constant principles; and when it is called the "universal ways" (dadao), does this not mean what is jointly followed in both ancient and modern times? In sum, although their names differ, their principle is one. What is called "reiterating and clarifying" (shenming) is that, lest anything remain unclear, one reiterates and clarifies it; what is called "carefully beautifying" (shenhui) is that, lest anything remain imperfect, one carefully makes it beautiful. Reverently spreading the teachings among the people is called "reverently spreading" (jingfu); calling it "beginning to cultivate" (zhaoxiu) is because…

… Jie had abandoned them and he began to restore them; prizing most highly the instruction of the people is called "prizing the people" (zhongmin); and calling it "that whereby they are ordered" (youxu) means wishing to know how the constant human relationships are brought into order. In sum, although the expressions differ in nuance, their substance is the same. Viewed in this light, that which rulers and ministers devote themselves to, that which sages and worthies have spoken of, that which is recorded in ancient and modern classics and commentaries, and the institutions created by the successive Sacred Emperors of our Dynasty—their similarities and differences are clear without waiting for debate. Ah! When human relationships are clarified above, the common people are affectionate below—this truly lies in the present day. How fortunate am I, in my simplicity, to witness it in person!

title: 天順四年會試錄
text:
考試官學士呂批策不為問目所窘根據事實條
荅無遺佳作也
對善為政者必以用人為本善用人者必以知
人為先為政而不用人則上有廢事用人而不
知人則下有遺才然則治天下者可不知人而
用之乎甚矣知人之難而用人之不易也在堯
之世而猶有靜言庸違方命圯族之共鯀仲康
之時而且有畔官離次俶擾天紀之羲和不謂
之難可乎在古且難况後世乎以知人言之高
===
帝之時漢室未危也而豫知周勃之能安劉氏
文帝之世七國未畔也而豫知亞夫之緩急可
任知人非不明也然而倖如審食其而不能去
賢如賈生而不能用何明於彼而暗於此耶唐
高祖於皇甫無逸知其清正為邪佞所構而劉
文靜無罪而被譖則不知也德宗於李藩望見
而知非作惡之人而陸贄以猜忌而廢黜則不
知也何得於彼而失於此耶張齊賢獻策宋太
祖知其可以為相用之可也而必留於異時李

If one governs without employing men, then above there will be neglected affairs; if one employs men without knowing them, then below there will be overlooked talents. That being so, can one who governs the world fail to know men and employ them? Great indeed is the difficulty of knowing men, and the challenge of employing them! Even in the age of Yao, there were still Gonggong and Gun, who spoke smoothly when quiet yet acted perversely when employed, and who defied commands and ruined their kin; in the time of Zhongkang, there were moreover Xi and He, who abandoned their offices, left their posts, and first threw the celestial regularities into confusion. Can this not be called difficult? If it was difficult even in antiquity, how much more so in later ages? Speaking in terms of knowing men: in the time of Emperor Gaozu [of Han], the House of Han was not yet in peril, yet he foresaw that Zhou Bo 周勃 would be able to secure the Liu clan; in the reign of Emperor Wen, the Seven States had not yet rebelled, yet he foresaw that [Zhou] Yafu 周亞夫 could be relied upon in an emergency. 於知人之道豈能盡審乎以用人言之漢高以

矣何以疑樊噲有附呂之謀宣帝知黃覇召為

之罪唐太宗棄魏徵之舊怨而處以諫議似矣

translation_en:
… Hang attended a banquet, Emperor Taizong (r. 976–997) knew that he could be entrusted with great responsibilities; he could have appointed him then, yet he insisted on waiting for a later day. As for [?] [王] Emperor Zhenzong (r. 997–1022), because of Wang Dan's (957–1017) memorials on state affairs, he knew that Wang could bring about great peace, yet when it came to the treacherous wickedness of Wang Qinruo (962–1025), he trusted him exclusively—why was this? Could these several rulers be said to have been completely discerning in the way of knowing men?

To speak in terms of employing men: Emperor Gaozu of Han (r. 202–195 BCE) regarded Zhang Liang (d. 186 BCE), Han Xin (d. 196 BCE), and Xiao He (d. 193 BCE) as the Three Heroes and ultimately employed them to accomplish his great enterprise—this was admirable; yet why did he suspect Fan Kuai (d. 189 BCE) of plotting to side with the Lü clan? Emperor Xuan (r. 74–48 BCE) recognized the worth of Huang Ba (130–51 BCE) and summoned him to serve as Case Reviewer in the Court of Judicial Review, whereupon the court praised his fairness—this was right; yet why did he inflict upon蓋 [Gai] Kuanrao (d. 60 BCE) the crime of "impiousness"? Emperor Taizong of Tang (r. 626–649) set aside his old grievances against Wei Zheng (580–643) and placed him in the post of Policy Adviser—this seemed fitting; yet why did he employ flatterers Who had served Yuwen Huaji (d. 619)? Emperor Xuanzong (r. 712–756), because Wang Qiu (d. 743) did not curry favor, promoted him to Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs—this was impartial; [yet why … (8 illegible characters)]? Eagerly set on great peace and holding his chief ministers responsible for results, so that the grandees congratulated one another that this surpassed divination by dreams and tortoise-shell, Emperor Renzong of Song (r. 1022–1063) employed men such as Wen Yanbo (1006–1097) and Fan Zhongyan (989–1052) appropriately; yet before long, on account of collective slander, he dismissed them all—was that appropriate? Summoning him as a Classical Lecturer, drawing upon his classical scholarship, and bestowing handwritten notes upon him in the utmost esteem and honor, Emperor Ningzong (r. 1194–1224) employed Master Zhu of Hui'an (Zhu Xi, 1130–1200) fittingly; yet before long, on charges of "spurious learning," he banished and drove him away—was that fitting? Could these several rulers, in turn, be said to have been completely appropriate in the way of employing men?

Alas! Although the various rulers of Han, Tang, and Song are said to have known men, they did not understand that knowing men has its essentials; although they are said to have employed men, they did not understand that employing men has its foundation. This is why their governance did not match that of antiquity.

title: 天順四年會試錄
text:
聖天子在上沈幾先物而有知人之明端本澄源而
盡取人之道是以内而居卿列者有都俞吁咈
之風外而居守令者多慈祥豈弟之善固足以
追蹤前古而下視漢唐宋矣然而不自滿假聖
人之心又豈肯自謂知之已明而用之悉當哉
故有以厪執事今日之問也誠使司薦舉者果
能如書所謂亦行有九德而有載采采之實則
下無遺材之歎司銓衡者果能如書所謂三德
浚明有家六德亮采有邦則才無枉用之失若
===
然則俊傑在位而庶績咸熈矣又何必徧詢諸
國人然後謂之公哉愚生不敢臆說姑摭古訓
以為明問之復執事尚毋謂其誦陳言而弗之

聖天子在上，沈幾先物而有知人之明，端本澄源而盡取人之道，是以内而居卿列者有都俞吁咈之風，外而居守令者多慈祥豈弟之善，固足以追蹤前古而下視漢、唐、宋矣。然而不自滿假，聖人之心又豈肯自謂知之已明而用之悉當哉？故有以厪執事今日之問也。誠使司薦舉者果能如《書》所謂「亦行有九德」，而有「載采采」之實，則下無遺材之歎；司銓衡者果能如《書》所謂「三德浚明有家，六德亮采有邦」，則才無枉用之失。若然，則俊傑在位而庶績咸熈矣，又何必徧詢諸國人，然後謂之公哉？愚生不敢臆說，姑摭古訓以為明問之復，執事尚毋謂其誦陳言而弗之采也。謹對。

第三問
陳選
同考試官編修丘批：策答從三代以前說來，末舉今日見行之事為斷，的有所見。知古知今，殆無愧於高第者乎！
同考試官編修王批：策能貫穿經史，馳騁古今，迹其
translation_en:
… our Sacred Son of Heaven reigns above, perceiving subtleincipiencies ahead of events and possessing the discernment to know men, rectifying the root and clarifying the source so as to fulfill completely the Way of selecting men. Therefore, within the court, those who occupy the ranks of Ministers display the spirit of harmonious assent and candid remonstrance ("du, yu, xu, fu"); outside in the provinces, those who serve as Prefects and Magistrates abound in the virtues of benevolence, kindness, and affability. Truly, this suffices to follow in the footsteps of remote antiquity and look down upon the Han, Tang, and Song dynasties! Yet, never self-satisfied or complacent, how could the mind of the Sage be willing to claim that his knowledge of men is already fully clear and his employment of them wholly fitting? That is why Your Excellency has been troubled to pose today's question.

If indeed those in charge of recommendations can truly act according to what the Book of Documents calls "in their conduct also possessing the Nine Virtues" and verify the reality of their "deeds and undertakings," then below there will be no sighing over neglected talent. And if those in charge of personnel evaluation and selection can truly act according to what the Book of Documents calls "displaying three virtues day by day to possess a family, and governing with six virtues to possess a state," then there will be no error of misusing talent. If this is so, then outstanding men of talent will occupy office and all official achievements will flourish in harmony; what need would there be to inquire everywhere among all the people of the state before calling it impartial?

This foolish student dares not offer unfounded conjectures, but merely gathers ancient precepts as a reply to your enlightened inquiry. May Your Excellency not say that I merely recite stale words and thus decline to adopt them! I respectfully reply.

Third Question
Chen Xuan

…what it says could not have been produced by anyone who did not already possess settled convictions in his breast. Selected to fill the quota, he will surely stand out among the literati.

Examiner Vice Minister Ke 柯 comments: All three sessions are excellent, and this policy essay along with the piece on current affairs differs especially from the other papers. Even without waiting for the legendary silent nod of approval, one should know that it meets the standard.

Examiner Academician Lü 呂 comments: He cites the moral integrity of the ancients and judges their sincerity or falsity, their successes and failures, as clearly as pointing to his own palm, while also knowing where to place the ultimate emphasis. Truly a man of broad learning and discernment! How could a high recommendation be undeserved?

Response: I have heard that when the ruler above establishes the state, he should attach great weight to reputation and integrity; when the subject below conducts himself, he should prize moral courage and principle. For when the state is established through reputation and integrity, the ethos of the literati will not become decadent; when one conducts oneself with moral courage and principle, the moral teachings will not be ruined. Is this not why incorruptibility and quiet modesty are the foremost priorities for those who possess a state, and the essential way for those who are scholars?

Reflecting on antiquity, when the court of Yu 虞 established its instruction, it said, "simple, yet incorrupt"; when the Offices of Zhou (Zhouguan 周官) evaluated officials, it said, "they are judged by their incorruptibility." How strict was the ruler's governance of the world! At that time, the greedy did not occupy office, and those who entered service did not do so on account of poverty. Scholars born in that age all knew self-respect; therefore, even a thousand teams of four horses or ten thousand measures of grain were insufficient to move their hearts.

Alas, the way of the world declined day by day, propriety and righteousness became obscured, and the ethos of climbing the mound to monopolize profit arose. Fortunately, amidst the collapsing waves and toppling billows, there were still men such as Zihan 子罕, Yang Zhen 楊震, Li Ji 李及, Bao Zheng 包拯, Kou Zhun 寇準, and Zhao Bian 趙抃. Therefore, taking "not being greedy as one's treasure" was not done to angle for fame; refusing gold in the dead of night was not out of fear that others would know. Buying a single literary collection was still regarded as shameful; taking away a single inkstone was still regarded as a stain. As for other examples, not replacing a worn bed-curtain was not to flaunt frugality before others; being accompanied only by a tortoise and a crane was not to display purity to others. punctuated: 其誠偽之分，奚啻天淵哉！古者井田法行，人皆務本；學校政舉，士皆守義。上之持世何備也！當是之時，士讓為大夫，大夫讓為卿。士生斯世，咸知自重，雖高爵厚祿，不足以介其意焉。奈何風俗日下，士習益卑，望塵而拜之風興矣。幸而風頽俗靡之餘，尚有若陳仲子、韋澳、錢若水、韓見素、司馬光、范鎮之諸公焉。是故辭相灌園，非好勞而惡逸；恥於呈身，不枉尺以直尋。急流勇退，何决也！未老掛冠，何果也！他如請歸西洛，非引以自高；不肯自陳，非甘為人下。其視荆舒之投老鍾山，其得失之辨，奚啻黑白哉！方今聖人在上，公道大明。邇者簡朝覲之臣庶，素行超卓者，則賜以襲衣，錫以宴勞，其旌異之典至矣。將見向之簠簋不飾者，莫不改行遷善，而為羔羊之大夫，尚何有登壟之餘風哉！因岩穴之遺老，隱居求志者，則聘以束帛，寵以璽書，其獎勸之意厚矣。將見向之馳騖苟進
translation_en: …the distinction between their sincerity and hypocrisy is no less than that between heaven and the abyss! In antiquity, when the well-field system was practiced, all people devoted themselves to fundamental occupations; when school administration was upheld, all scholars abided by righteousness. How complete was the rulers' maintenance of the world! At that time, servicemen yielded the rank of Grand Master to one another, and Grand Masters yielded the rank of Minister. Scholars born in that age all knew self-respect, so that even high noble rank and generous emoluments were insufficient to weigh upon their minds. How regrettable that as customs declined day by day and the habits of scholars grew ever more base, the practice of bowing at the sight of a patron's dust arose! Fortunately, amid the decadent winds and degenerate customs, there were still worthies such as Chen Zhongzi 陳仲子, Wei Ao 韋澳, Qian Ruoshui 錢若水, Han Jiansu 韓見素 (Han亿/Han Wei), Sima Guang 司馬光, and Fan Zhen 范鎮. Therefore, declining a premiership to water gardens was not out of a fondness for toil and a dislike of ease; being ashamed to thrust oneself forward was refusing to bend a foot in order to straighten eight feet. Retiring bravely from a rushing stream—how decisive! Hanging up one's official cap before old age—how resolute! As for others: requesting to return to Western Luoyang (Xiluo 西洛) was not withdrawing to exalt oneself; refusing to plead one's own case was not being content to remain beneath others. Compared with Jing Shu 荆舒 (Wang Anshi 王安石) retiring in old age to Mount Zhong (Zhongshan 鍾山), the distinction between their right and wrong is no less than that between black and white! Right now, the Sage is on the throne, and the Way of impartiality shines brightly. Recently, in selecting among the officials who came for court audience, those whose habitual conduct was outstanding were bestowed suits of robes and rewarded with banquets for their toil—the ceremonies for honoring the exceptional have reached the utmost! We shall soon see that those who formerly failed to keep their sacrificial vessels in order (i.e., who were corrupt) will all reform their conduct and move toward goodness, becoming Grand Masters like those in the ode "Lambskin" (Gaoyang 羔羊); what lingering habit of climbing mounds to monopolize profit could still remain? We shall soon see that those who formerly galloped about seeking advancement by any means…

This being so, how could either of the two be neglected in favor of the other? I have ventured to discuss this: the ways of governance are two—administration and education, nothing more. punctuated: 一有偏廢，則徒善不足以為政，徒法不能以自行矣。是故防邊也、審刑也、恤窮也、弭盜也、通漕也、救荒也，此六者皆所謂政事也；革浮薄也、驅異端也、率游惰也、崇孝愛也，此四者皆所謂教化也。方今聖天子在上，以《關雎》、《麟趾》之化，而行《周官》之法度，本末具舉，政教兼施，而於是數者尚有未甚效者，何耶？非法度之不立也，非教化之不行也，正以奉行者之不得其人故耳。使守邊之將，皆如趙充國之圖上方略，則邊塵息矣；治獄之吏，皆如徐有功之以恕求情，則刑獄清矣。得人以賑恤，如富弼之在青州，尚何鰥寡失所之足慮乎？得人以禁捕，如虞詡之在朝歌，尚何盜賊未弭之足虞乎？以至救荒而得耿壽昌，漕運而得劉晏，又何患荒政之不舉，而國用之不足乎？夫事之小者，固在於得人，況乎事之有大於此者乎？使革浮薄者，皆如子游之為武城宰，而教以禮樂，則浮薄可變而為敦龐矣；闢異端者，皆如韓愈…
translation_en: If either is neglected in favor of the other, then goodness alone is insufficient for governance, and laws alone cannot carry themselves into effect. Therefore, defending the frontiers, reviewing punishments, relieving the destitute, suppressing bandits, keeping the grain transport flowing, and relieving famine—these six are all what are called administrative affairs. Reforming frivolity and shallowness, expelling heterodoxies, leading the idle and lazy, and exalting filial piety and fraternal affection—these four are all what is called moral transformation through education. At present, the Sacred Son of Heaven reigns above; with the transformative influence of the "Cry of the Osprey" (Guanju) and the "Feet of the Unicorn" (Linzhi), he carries out the laws and institutions of the Offices of Zhou (Zhouguan). Root and branch are both upheld, and administration and education are simultaneously applied. Yet in these several matters, why have they still not proved entirely effective? It is not that laws and institutions are not established, nor that moral transformation is not practiced; it is precisely because those who carry them out are not the right men. If the generals defending the frontiers were all like Zhao Chongguo 趙充國 submitting mapped-out strategies to the throne, then the dust of border warfare would subside. If the officials trying legal cases were all like Xu Yougong 徐有功 seeking the truth of the circumstances with empathetic consideration, then punishments and litigation would be clear and fair. If we obtained the right men to provide relief, like Fu Bi 富弼 in Qingzhou 青州, what cause would there still be to worry about widowers and widows losing their livelihoods? If we obtained the right men to prohibit and apprehend criminals, like Yu Xu 虞詡 in Zhaoge 朝歌, what cause would there still be to fear that bandits and thieves are not suppressed? And if, furthermore, for famine relief we obtained a Geng Shouchang 耿壽昌, and for grain transport we obtained a Liu Yan 劉晏, why would we worry that famine relief administration is not carried out or that state finances are insufficient? Now, if lesser affairs certainly depend upon obtaining the right men, how much more so do affairs that are greater than these? If those who reform frivolity and shallowness were all like Ziyou 子游 serving as Magistrate of Wucheng 武城 and teaching the people with rites and music, then frivolity and shallowness could be transformed into sincerity and solidity. If those who refute heterodoxies were all like Han Yu 韓愈…

義矣召信臣守南陽而出入阡陌得人如此則
游惰之徒寧不勤於耕桑乎子皐為成宰而民
遂為其兄衰得人如此則食稻衣錦之輩寧不
興於孝愛乎孔子曰為政在人是人又為修政
立教之本也盖得其人則事之大小無不舉矣
非謂但行其大者而小者不足恤也愚也於天
下之事固有所未知而於天下之書則粗讀其
一二矣今承明問故敢以孔子得人之說進焉
===

… presenting the "Memorial on the Bone of the Buddha" (Føgu biao) and vigorously refuting the opinions of the crowd, then heterodox teachings could be driven out and people returned to ritual and righteousness. Shao Xinchen served as Governor of Nanyang and went out and about among the field paths; if one obtains men like this, how could the idle and lazy not become diligent in plowing and sericulture? Zigao served as Magistrate of Cheng and the people consequently wore mourning garments for their elder brothers; if one obtains men like this, how could those who eat fine rice and wear brocade not be inspired to filial piety and fraternal love? Confucius said, "Governance lies in getting the right men." Thus, men are furthermore the foundation for cultivating governance and establishing instruction. Indeed, if one obtains the right men, then affairs both great and small will all be successfully carried out; it does not mean that one should only attend to great affairs while small affairs are not worth heeding. Ignorant as I am, there are certainly things among the affairs of the world that I do not yet know, though among the books of the world I have roughly read one or two. Now, having received your enlightened question, I therefore dare to present Confucius's doctrine of obtaining the right men. As for trafficking in impractical and stagnant talk that is of no benefit to the affairs of the empire and the state, that is not my long-held aspiration. I respectfully reply.

Fifth Question
Lou Fang 婁芳

title: 天順四年會試錄
text:
考試官學士呂批敬字訓釋易曉而用力實難此策
條答詳盡其知所以用力者與
對敬一也經傳之所載者各有所指聖賢之所
論者各有所見盖各有所指故其言殊各有所
見故其說異然其為敬則一而已夫豈可泥其
言之不同而致疑哉愚請稽諸經傳以明之書
稱堯曰欽明允恭稱舜但曰温恭盖史臣随事
而賛之耳堯舜皆聖人也孰謂舜於欽有未能
乎詩稱湯曰聖敬日躋稱文王曰緝熈敬止乃
===
詩人随事而美之耳湯文亦聖人也孰謂於欽
恭有未盡乎敬義皆存諸中者而易云敬以直
内義以方外雖若可疑殊不知義形而外方非
若告子義外之謂也莊肅見於容者而禮云心
莊則體舒心肅則容敬似有可議殊不知積中
而發外非若小人色厲之比也以是敬而脩身
則德萃於身故臼季曰敬者德之聚能敬必有
德以是敬而奉祭則神必享其祭故劉康公曰
勤禮莫如致敬敬在養神孔子答弟子問仁告

勤禮莫如致敬敬在養神孔子荅弟子問仁告
punctuated:
考試官學士呂批：敬字訓釋易曉，而用力實難。此策條答詳盡，其知所以用力者與！

對：敬一也，經傳之所載者各有所指，聖賢之所論者各有所見。盖各有所指，故其言殊；各有所見，故其說異。然其為敬，則一而已。夫豈可泥其言之不同而致疑哉？愚請稽諸《經》、傳以明之。《書》稱堯曰「欽明允恭」，稱舜但曰「温恭」，盖史臣随事而賛之耳。堯、舜皆聖人也，孰謂舜於欽有未能乎？《詩》稱湯曰「聖敬日躋」，稱文王曰「緝熈敬止」，乃詩人随事而美之耳。湯、文亦聖人也，孰謂於欽恭有未盡乎？敬、義皆存諸中者，而《易》云「敬以直内，義以方外」，雖若可疑，殊不知義形而外方，非若告子「義外」之謂也。莊、肅見於容者，而《禮》云「心莊則體舒，心肅則容敬」，似有可議，殊不知積中而發外，非若小人「色厲」之比也。以是敬而脩身，則德萃於身，故臼季曰：「敬者，德之聚。能敬必有德。」以是敬而奉祭，則神必享其祭，故劉康公曰：「勤禮莫如致敬，敬在養神。」孔子答弟子問仁，告
translation_en:
Examiner and Academician Lü comments: The glosses on the word "reverence" (jing 敬) are easy to understand, yet applying effort to it in practice is truly difficult. This policy essay answers item by item in exhaustive detail; surely the candidate is one who knows how to apply such effort!

Response: Reverence is one and the same. What is recorded in the Classics and commentaries each has its specific reference, and what is discussed by the sages and worthies each has its particular perspective. Because each has its specific reference, their words differ; because each has its particular perspective, their explanations vary. Yet as for being reverence, it is simply one. How could one cling rigidly to the differences in their words and harbour doubts? I beg leave to examine the Classics and commentaries to clarify this. The Book of Documents (Shu 書) praises Yao by saying he was "reverent, intelligent, and sincerely courteous" (qinming yungong 欽明允恭), while praising Shun only as "mild and courteous" (wengong 温恭); this is simply that the historiographers praised them in accordance with specific matters. Yao and Shun were both sages—who would say that Shun was incapable of reverence (qin 欽)? The Book of Odes (Shi 詩) praises Tang by saying "his sagely reverence daily ascended" (shengjing riji 聖敬日躋), and praises King Wen by saying "continuing and bright was his reverent resting" (jixi jingzhi 緝熈敬止); this is simply that the poets extolled them in accordance with specific matters. Tang and King Wen were also sages—who would say that they fell short of utmost reverence and courtesy (qingong 欽恭)? Reverence and righteousness (yi 義) both reside within, yet the Book of Changes (Yi 易) says, "Reverence to straighten the interior, righteousness to square the exterior." Although this might seem doubtful, one fails to realize that when righteousness takes form, the exterior is made square—it is not what Gaozi 告子 meant by "righteousness is external." Solemnity (zhuang 莊) and gravity (su 肅) are manifested in one's countenance, yet the Book of Rites (Li 禮) says, "When the mind is solemn, the body is at ease; when the mind is grave, the countenance is reverent." Although this seems open to question, one fails to realize that what accumulates within isを発 manifested without—it is not comparable to the petty man's "putting on a stern countenance." When one cultivates the self with this reverence, virtue gathers in the self; therefore Jiu Ji 臼季 said: "Reverence is the gathering of virtue. One who can be reverent will surely possess virtue." When one offers sacrifices with this reverence, the spirits will surely enjoy the sacrifice; therefore Duke Kang of Liu 劉康公 said: "In diligently performing the rites, nothing is better than utmost reverence; reverence lies in nourishing the spirits." title: 天順四年會試錄
text:
以出門使民居處執事之敬者非謂敬即仁盖
能敬則心存理得而為仁之功不外是也子思
論道不可離繼以戒慎恐懼慎獨之敬者非謂
敬即道盖能敬則靜存動察而體道之功在於
此也程子曰主一之謂敬無適之謂一此以心
要專一不以他念雜之而言曰整齊嚴肅則心
便一此以貌當尊嚴自無非僻干之而言內外
交養如此則持敬之功始備矣曰涵養須用敬
以存養本原而言曰進學則在致知以思索義
===
理而言工夫並進如此則主敬之功益密矣至
其門人謝上蔡謂敬是常惺惺法盖言心無所
昧敬而明也尹和靖謂敬者其心收斂不容一
物盖言心無所撓敬而專也與程子之言盖互
相發明寧有背戾哉由是觀之始焉入德由敬
而入終焉成德由敬而成安人安百姓在此聰
明睿智出於此事天饗帝本於此君子無所不
用其敬誠有如執事所言者愚也晚進末學雖
於聖賢之敬未知所入然於朱子晚年畏字之

punctuated: 以出門、使民、居處、執事之敬者，非謂敬即仁，盖能敬則心存理得，而為仁之功不外是也。子思論道不可離，繼以戒慎、恐懼、慎獨之敬者，非謂敬即道，盖能敬則靜存動察，而體道之功在於此也。程子曰：「主一之謂敬，無適之謂一。」此以心要專一，不以他念雜之而言。曰：「整齊嚴肅則心便一。」此以貌當尊嚴，自無非僻干之而言。內外交養如此，則持敬之功始備矣。曰：「涵養須用敬。」以存養本原而言。曰：「進學則在致知。」以思索義理而言。工夫並進如此，則主敬之功益密矣。至其門人謝上蔡謂「敬是常惺惺法」，盖言心無所昧，敬而明也；尹和靖謂「敬者，其心收斂，不容一物」，盖言心無所撓，敬而專也。與程子之言盖互相發明，寧有背戾哉！由是觀之，始焉入德，由敬而入；終焉成德，由敬而成。安人、安百姓在此，聰明睿智出於此，事天、饗帝本於此。君子無所不用其敬，誠有如執事所言者。愚也晚進末學，雖於聖賢之敬未知所入，然於朱子晚年畏字之
translation_en: …with the reverence of going abroad, employing the common people, dwelling in retirement, and handling affairs—this does not mean that reverence is itself humaneness, for when one is able to be reverent, the mind is preserved and principle is attained, so the effort of practicing humaneness lies in nothing beyond this. When Zisi 子思 discussed how the Way cannot be departed from, and followed it with the reverence of being cautious, apprehensive, and watchful over oneself when alone—this does not mean that reverence is itself the Way, for when one is able to be reverent, one preserves the mind in quiescence and examines oneself in activity, so the effort of embodying the Way lies herein. Master Cheng 程子 said: "Concentrating on one thing is called reverence; going nowhere else is called being one." This speaks of how the mind must be focused and unified, not adulterated by other thoughts. He also said: "When one is orderly, composed, grave, and solemn, the mind instantly becomes unified." This speaks of how one's demeanor ought to be dignified and austere, so that naturally no improper or perverse influences can intrude upon it. When the inner and outer mutually nourish one another like this, the effort of maintaining reverence is finally complete. He said: "For nurturing the mind, one must employ reverence." This speaks with reference to preserving and nourishing the fundamental source. And he said: "Advancing in learning lies in extending knowledge." This speaks with reference to pondering and investigating moral principles. When both efforts advance together like this, the work of holding to reverence becomes ever more thorough. As for his disciples, Xie Shangcai 謝上蔡 (Xie Liangzuo 謝良佐) said that "reverence is the method of staying constantly alert and awake," which means the mind is nowhere darkened, being reverent and therefore luminous; Yin Hejing 尹和靖 (Yin Tun 尹焞) said that "as for reverence, the mind is gathered in and admits not a single thing," which means the mind is nowhere disturbed, being reverent and therefore focused. These sayings and the words of Master Cheng mutually elucidate one another—how could there be any contradiction between them! Viewed in this light, in the beginning when entering into virtue, one enters through reverence; in the end when bringing virtue to completion, one completes it through reverence. Bringing peace to others and peace to all the people lies in this; acute hearing, clear sight, and penetrating wisdom emerge from this; serving Heaven and making offerings to the Supreme Lord are rooted in this. That the noble man leaves no place where he does not employ his reverence is truly just as you, the Examiners, have stated. Though I am a junior scholar of shallow learning and do not yet know the way of entry into the reverence of the sages and worthies, nevertheless, regarding Master Zhu's 朱子 (Zhu Xi 朱熹) late-life teaching on the word "awe" (wei 畏)…

會試錄後序

皇上光復寶位以来，天下事無小大，咸蚤夜究圖，更張敝弛，以復祖宗之弘規；而於科目一事，尤勤于聖慮。蓋以士為治本，科目為得士之門，重科目而精於取士，則以天下才理天下事，其致治為不難矣。天順庚辰春，胄監之士及四方偕計吏以升者餘三千人。禮部以聞，請官主考會試。上以命臣原，而臣潛亦與焉。既涖
translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

Since His Majesty gloriously restored the Precious Throne, in all affairs of the realm, whether great or small, he has examined and planned from morning till night, reforming what had grown corrupt and lax so as to restore the grand regulations of the Imperial Ancestors; and to the matter of the civil service examinations, he has devoted especially diligent imperial thought. For scholars are the foundation of governance, and the examination system is the gateway to obtaining scholars. When one attaches importance to the examinations and exercises precision in selecting scholars, then by employing the talents of the realm to manage the affairs of the realm, achieving good governance is not difficult.

In the spring of the gengchen year of the Tianshun era (1460), scholars from the Directorate of Education and those from the four quarters who were advanced along with the tribute-reporting officials numbered more than three thousand men. The Ministry of Rites reported this to the throne and requested officials to serve as chief examiners for the Metropolitan Examination. 十人蓋精選也仰惟

punctuated: 事，凡三試之，得士如美木之宜材、嘉穀之可薦食者百五十人，蓋精選也。仰惟國朝列聖相承，脩明文教，環九區薄海內外，咸被帝德光華，士之生，幸得其時也；育於庠序，陶於詩書，而進以科目之榮，士之出，幸得其途也；皇上勵精圖治，其於賢且能者，求之惟恐不及，則士之仕，又幸得其君也。負此三幸，豈可徒自幸乎？尚亦思為
translation_en: … my duties, and examined them across three sessions in all, obtaining one hundred and fifty scholars who are like fine trees suited for timber and excellent grain fit to be offered as food—truly a careful selection. Looking up in reflection, the successive sacred emperors of our dynasty have inherited the throne one after another, cultivating and illuminating civil teachings. Across the nine regions and within and beyond the four seas, all are bathed in the glorious splendor of imperial virtue; thus, in their birth, scholars are fortunate to have met with the right time. Nurtured in the state schools, molded by the Odes and Documents, and advancing through the honor of the examination system, in their emergence into public life, scholars are fortunate to have found the right path. His Majesty the Emperor devotes his utmost energy to governance, and in seeking out those who are worthy and capable, his only fear is failing to reach them; thus, in serving in office, scholars are furthermore fortunate to have found the right ruler. Bearing these three good fortunes, how could they merely rejoice for themselves? Rather, they should also think of being…

title: 天順四年會試錄
text:
國家幸也廉以宅心勤以集事
百凡之寄我者寧勞焉不欲
逸而我之取直寧不及焉不
使有餘斯幸矣然此猶以筮
仕言之若夫荐沐
休恩躋于穹秩攄弘謨以贊大
化使天下民物熙和上侔唐
===
虞之治又非
國家之大幸與其或不幸有喔
咿儒兒以徼寵者有荒惰闇
昧以廢事者有蓬心蒿目肆
貪墨而喪名檢者皆為士之
羞也爾諸賢士將奉對
大廷以有官序也用書此為規

===
虞之治又非
國家之大幸與其或不幸有喔
咿嚅唲以徼寵者有荒情闇
昧以廢事者有蓬心蒿目肆
貪墨而喪名檢者皆爲士之
羞也爾諸賢士將奉對
大廷以有官序也用書此爲規
punctuated: 國家幸也！廉以宅心，勤以集事。百凡之寄我者，寧勞焉不欲逸；而我之取直，寧不及焉不使有餘，斯幸矣。然此猶以筮仕言之。若夫荐沐休恩，躋于穹秩，攄弘謨以贊大化，使天下民物熙和，上侔唐虞之治，又非國家之大幸與？其或不幸，有喔咿儒兒以徼寵者，有荒惰闇昧以廢事者，有蓬心蒿目肆貪墨而喪名檢者，皆為士之羞也。爾諸賢士，將奉對大廷，以有官序也，用書此為規，
translation_en: … a fortunate blessing for the state! Anchor your minds in integrity, and accomplish your duties through diligence. In all matters entrusted to us, rather bear the toil than desire ease; and in receiving our emoluments, rather take less than allow a surplus—this indeed will be fortunate. Yet this speaks only of the beginning of one's official career. As for repeatedly bathing in the gracious favor of the throne and ascending to exalted ranks, unfolding grand plans to assist in the great transformation, so that the people and all things under heaven live in prosperous harmony, rivaling above the governance of Tang and Yu [Yao and Shun]—would this not be an even greater fortune for the state? Should it unfortunately happen that there are those who force obsequious smiles and act like fawning children to curry favor, those who are negligent, indolent, and benighted to the detriment of public affairs, or those with weed-choked minds and nearsighted eyes who indulge in rapacity and corruption and ruin their reputation and moral conduct—all such men are a disgrace to scholars. All you worthy scholars are about to present your replies in the Great Court [the Palace Examination] and thereby enter official rank; therefore, I write this as an admonition…
